==== Apple TV Home Videos (Life) https://que.one/life/appletv-videos.html
Kind: howto

## Home Videos Via Apple TV

Share MP4 videos on a Mac with an Apple TV through the [Apple TV app](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_TV_app) on the Mac:

1. Open the Apple TV app on the Mac and choose *File > Import…* to add the folder holding the videos.
2. Open *System Settings > General > Sharing* and turn on **Media Sharing**.
3. Click the **(i)** icon next to Media Sharing to name the library and choose what to share.
4. Put the Mac and the Apple TV on the same Wi-Fi network.
5. Sign in with the same Apple ID on the Apple TV if prompted.

The Mac must stay powered on to serve the videos.

==== Baseball (Life) https://que.one/life/baseball.html
Kind: take

## Baseball

To me, [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball) is an American art form. I am not the first to say so. In Ken Burns' [Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball_(TV_series)), [Gerald Early](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Early) named the Constitution, jazz, and baseball as the three most [beautifully designed](https://clintonwhitehouse6.archives.gov/1994/09/1994-09-22-remarks-by-president-at-rhythm-and-blues-concert.html) things American culture has produced. Three things make the design [beautiful](../mind/beauty.md) to me.

First, the game has no game clock. It ends in outs, not minutes, which is why [George Carlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Carlin) called it a [pastoral game](https://www.sfgate.com/sports/article/george-carlin-bit-is-still-a-classic-4723368.php). That flow survived the [pitch clock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_clock) Major League Baseball added in 2023, which times only the gap between pitches. It cut about half an hour from the average game, and only a die-hard purist misses that half hour.

Second, it is many games inside one. The pitcher duels the hitter, the managers try to outguess each other, and the fans needle each other in the stands. That makes it a game of strategy and a lot of fun.

Third, almost every fan inherits a thread of history with it. A father, an uncle, or a grandfather loved a team or hated a player, and the feeling gets passed down. No other realm holds that much nostalgia for me.

It is also America's gift to the world, though the gift took root mostly around the Caribbean and in East Asia. John Fogerty's "[Centerfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centerfield_(song))" tips its cap to Chuck Berry's "Brown Eyed Handsome Man," and I tip mine to both.

For data hacking, I keep one link: <https://github.com/baseballhackday/data-and-resources/wiki/Resources-and-ideas>

==== Blood Pressure Diet (Life) https://que.one/life/bp-diet.html
Kind: reference

## Blood Pressure Diet

A cheat-sheet in the spirit of the [DASH diet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DASH_diet), the eating pattern most guidelines recommend for lowering blood pressure.

### Quick Bits
- Remember that the [kidneys are the body’s primary long-term regulators of blood pressure](kidneys-bp.md).
- Choose fresh or minimally processed foods.
- Rinse canned beans and vegetables to reduce sodium.
- Use herbs, spices, lemon, and vinegar instead of salt.
- Aim for mostly home-cooked meals.

### Foods That Help Lower or Prevent High Blood Pressure

| Category | Examples |
|--------|---------|
| **Potassium-Rich Foods** | Bananas, oranges & citrus, avocados, tomatoes, beans & lentils, sweet potatoes, spinach, kale, Swiss chard |
| **Vegetables & Greens** | Beets / beet juice, arugula, broccoli, mixed vegetables |
| **Whole Grains** | Oats, quinoa, whole-grain breads & cereals |
| **Healthy Fats** | Olive oil, nuts & seeds, salmon, sardines, mackerel |
| **Low-Fat Dairy** | Yogurt, kefir, low-fat milk |

### Foods to Limit or Avoid

| Category | Examples |
|--------|---------|
| **High-Sodium Foods** | Canned soups, frozen meals, fast food, deli meats, bacon, sausage, soy sauce, teriyaki sauce |
| **Processed Snacks** | Chips, instant noodles, packaged baked goods |
| **Sugary Foods & Drinks** | Soda, desserts, sweetened coffee drinks |
| **Excess Alcohol & Caffeine** | More than 1–2 drinks/day, excess energy drinks or coffee (if BP-sensitive) |
| **Unhealthy Fats** | Fried foods, processed meats, foods containing trans fats |

==== Chess (Life) https://que.one/life/chess.html

## Chess

Openings I want to master, each linked to its [chess opening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_opening) page.

For White:

- [King's Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Gambit), especially the [Muzio Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muzio_Gambit)
- [Danish Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Gambit)
- [Fried Liver Attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fried_Liver_Attack)
- [Cochrane Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrov%27s_Defence#Classical_Variation:_3.Nxe5)
- [Scotch Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotch_Gambit)
- [Halloween Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween_Gambit)
- [Monkey's Bum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Defense#Monkey%27s_Bum), the spiciest of the lot
- [Hillbilly Attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caro%E2%80%93Kann_Defence#Hillbilly_Attack) against the Caro-Kann
- [Ponziani Opening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponziani_Opening)

For Black:

- [Latvian Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latvian_Gambit)

### PGN cleanup

Strip the clock stamps and repeated move numbers from a [PGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portable_Game_Notation) file exported from chess.com:

```bash
pgnconv() {
    cat $1 | sed  "s/ \[%timestamp null\]//g" | sed "s/ [0-9]*\.\.\.//g" > ${1%.*}_2.pgn
}
```

## Columbo
![Columbo](columbo.jpg)

The 69 episodes of [Columbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Columbo_episodes), as transcoded from the Complete Series DVD set. The other watch list here is [Star Wars Chronology](star-wars.md).

Anyone who owns that set can use [HandBrake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HandBrake) ([download](https://handbrake.fr/)) to transcode each title to MP4 and stream it locally:

```bash
HandBrakeCLI -Z "Fast 480p30" -i /Volumes/COLUMBO -t 2 --no-two-pass -o FILENAME.mp4
```

`-t` is the title number on each disc, typically 1, 2, or 3.

==== Compatibility (Life) https://que.one/life/compatibility.html
Kind: take

## Compatibility

I think romantic compatibility runs on the same [three realms](../mind/three-realms.md) as the rest of life: the physical, the emotional, and the intellectual. A lasting match needs fit in all three, though not a perfect one. In love, fit in each realm is a matter of taste and feeling. Robert Sternberg's [triangular theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangular_theory_of_love), the best-known model of love, also has three parts: intimacy, passion, and commitment. It leaves out the intellect, and it leaves out luck.

The order of the realms matters a little too. Partners who rank the realms the same way may get along more easily. The similarity evidence says not to lean on that. A [meta-analysis of 313 studies](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0265407508096700) found that actual similarity stopped predicting attraction once people were in a relationship. Perceived similarity still predicted it.

The fourth factor is serendipity, the luck that brings two people together. It is not a realm, because it is not something a mind does. The three realms describe the fit, but luck decides whether two people meet at all, and when. Plain nearness shapes who pairs up, which psychologists call the [propinquity effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propinquity). Fit is also hard to foresee. In a [2017 speed-dating study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28853645/), over 100 measures of traits and preferences could not predict which specific pairs would want each other.

So I see the three realms as the part of compatibility we can judge once we meet, and luck as the part we cannot. Luck is partly built, as [Personal Growth](personal-growth.md) argues. It still gets a vote.

==== Crop Videos (Life) https://que.one/life/crop-videos.html
Kind: howto

## Cropping Videos

Crop the sides of a widescreen clip (16:9) down to the old 4:3 movie shape with [FFmpeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FFmpeg):

```bash
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vf "crop=ih*4/3:ih:(iw-ih*4/3)/2:0" -t 5 -c:a copy output.mp4
```

- `-i input.mp4`: the input video file.
- `-vf "crop=ih*4/3:ih:(iw-ih*4/3)/2:0"`: the crop filter.
  - `ih` is the input height.
  - `ih*4/3` is the new width that keeps a 4:3 aspect ratio.
  - `(iw-ih*4/3)/2` centers the crop horizontally.
- `-t 5`: optional; keeps only the first 5 seconds.
- `-c:a copy`: copies the audio stream without re-encoding.
- `output.mp4`: the output file.

To put a song under the clip instead, see [Mix Music Into a Video](mix-music-video.md).

==== Decrypt Disc to MKV (Life) https://que.one/life/disc-to-mkv.html
Kind: howto

## Decrypt Disc to MKV File

1. Rip the Blu-ray or DVD with the [MakeMKV](https://www.makemkv.com/) desktop app, installed with `brew`. The resulting [MKV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matroska) file keeps the disc's full quality, which makes it the cleanest archival format.
2. Convert the MKV to MP4 so the Apple TV app plays it as a [home video](appletv-videos.md):

```bash
ffmpeg -i input.mkv -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -c:v copy -c:a ac3 -b:a 640k output.mp4
```

==== Engaging Strangers (Life) https://que.one/life/engaging-strangers.html
Kind: howto

## Engaging Strangers

Most of us would rather not talk to strangers, and most of us are wrong about it. Commuters asked to talk with a stranger [enjoyed the ride more](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25019381/) than those who kept to themselves, though people expected the opposite. After a conversation, people [underestimate how much the other person liked them](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30183512/). The steps below lower the cost of the first move for both sides.

1. **Collapse anonymity fast.** Make brief eye contact and give a small smile or an [eyebrow flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyebrow_flash). Stand slightly angled, not squared up, so the approach does not read as a challenge.
2. **Introduce a shared frame.** Make an observation about something you can both see, not an opinion. No questions and nothing personal yet. Simply narrate reality.
3. **Lower the response burden.** Give them several off-ramps. Paradoxically, reminding people they are free to say no [tends to raise](https://open.lnu.se/index.php/metapsychology/article/download/2640/3402) the chance they say yes.
4. **Signal an easy exit.** Keep your feet and body pointed toward what you were already doing.
5. **Escalate only after reciprocity.** No signal, no escalation. Once they respond, a question is welcome, and a [follow-up question](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28447835/) makes people like you more.
6. **Mirror once.** If they agree briefly, echo it: "Yeah. Brutal."
7. **Go further only if they add something of their own.** A short answer is a polite close. Take it.

==== Flourishing (Life) https://que.one/life/flourishing.html
Kind: take

## Flourishing

Henri Bergson called it the [élan vital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89lan_vital), a force that drives life forward. Science dropped the force, but I keep the phrase. What drives me is no mystical force. It is the [seeking system](../mind/transcendence.md), the itch to explore and expect, and flourishing is where I point it.

I point it six ways:

- **Physical comfort:** the richness of material life, attuned to vitality.
- **Emotional depth:** the full range of connection and inner harmony.
- **Intellectual clarity:** curiosity and the joy of understanding.
- **Humor and grace:** gentle, sharp, attuned to joy and absurdity.
- **Spiritual depth:** meaning and presence, in a secular sense.
- **Social nurture:** trust and care.

The first three are the [three realms](../mind/three-realms.md), and my ranking of them is still temperament. Flourishing does not mean equal effort. It means none of the six goes dark. Humor and spiritual depth are my additions, and the standard [catalog of character strengths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_Strengths_and_Virtues) files both under transcendence.

The practice is a loop. Refine what the six mean to me. Pursue them with courage and humility, head up. [Accept](personal-growth.md) that I will never arrive, since [things fall apart](../mind/core-challenges.md) and the [hedonic treadmill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedonic_treadmill) resets every gain. Watch for distraction and drift, which is the [pause](../mind/reflexivity.md) at work, and realign with my values. Then start again, because desires change.

What matters is direction, not arrival.

==== Growing Old (Life) https://que.one/life/growing-old.html
Kind: quote

## Growing Old

The best answer to the fear of death I have read is this passage from "How to Grow Old" in [Portraits from Memory and Other Essays](https://archive.org/details/portraitsfrommem00russrich) by [Bertrand Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_Russell):

> The best way to overcome it [*the fear of death*] — so at least it seems to me — is to make your interests gradually wider and more impersonal, until bit by bit the walls of the ego recede, and your life becomes increasingly merged in the universal life. *An individual human existence should be like a river*: small at first, narrowly contained within its banks, and rushing passionately past rocks and over waterfalls. Gradually the river grows wider, the banks recede, the waters flow more quietly, and in the end, without any visible break, they become merged in the sea, and painlessly lose their individual being. The man who, in old age, can see his life in this way, will not suffer from the fear of death, since the things he cares for will continue. And if, with the decay of vitality, weariness increases, the thought of rest will not be unwelcome. I should wish to die while still at work, knowing that others will carry on what I can no longer do and content in the thought that what was possible has been done.

==== Converting iPhone Ringtones (Life) https://que.one/life/iphone-ringtones.html
Kind: howto

## Converting iPhone Ringtones

Every conversion below is one [FFmpeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FFmpeg) command; an iPhone [ringtone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ringtone) is an M4R file of 40 seconds or less.

- Convert ringtone M4R to MP3: `ffmpeg -i input.m4r -acodec libmp3lame -ab 256k output.mp3`
- Convert MP3 to ringtone M4R (must be 40s or less): `ffmpeg -i input.mp3 -t 40 -acodec aac -b:a 256k -f ipod output.m4r`
- Convert WAV to ringtone M4R (must be 40s or less): `ffmpeg -i input.wav -acodec aac -b:a 256k -f ipod output.m4r`
- Read M4R metadata: `ffmpeg -i yourfile.m4r` or `ffprobe -v quiet -print_format json -show_format -show_streams yourfile.m4r`
- Change M4R metadata without re-encoding, repeating `-metadata` as needed: `ffmpeg -i yourfile.m4r -metadata title="My Ringtone" -c copy -f ipod output.m4r`

==== Kidneys and Blood Pressure (Life) https://que.one/life/kidneys-bp.html
Kind: note

## Kidneys and Blood Pressure

I keep this page for the part that diet advice tends to skip. The kidneys are the body's main long-term control for blood pressure. They set it over days and years. They do this by changing blood volume, releasing hormones, and nudging the tone of blood vessels. In a healthy body their default job is to get rid of extra sodium and water.

### Volume control

The kidneys match how much sodium and water they pass to the current pressure. This loop is called pressure [natriuresis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natriuresis). When pressure rises, they pass more sodium and water, and blood volume shrinks. When pressure falls, they hold on to both, and volume grows.

### The renin cascade

When blood flow to the kidneys drops, or sodium falls, the kidneys release renin. Renin starts the [renin–angiotensin system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renin%E2%80%93angiotensin_system). Angiotensin II tightens blood vessels. Aldosterone holds on to sodium and water. Vasopressin holds on to water. The result is higher pressure.

### Vessel signaling

The kidneys also make local signals that adjust the width of blood vessels. Prostaglandins and nitric oxide widen them. Endothelin narrows them.

### What that means for diet

Sodium is the lever a person can pull. Eating less [salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_effects_of_salt) lowers blood pressure in most people who have high blood pressure. That is the sourced advice behind the [blood pressure diet](bp-diet.md). For [low blood pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypotension) that lasts, the usual advice is the reverse. Drink enough water, and do not cut sodium without a reason.

### Why it matters

[Hypertensive kidney disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertensive_kidney_disease) is the loop turning on itself. Kidney disease raises blood pressure. High pressure that goes untreated damages the kidneys. So protecting the kidneys is part of keeping pressure under control for the long run.

==== Legacy (Life) https://que.one/life/legacy.html
Kind: take

## Legacy

The wish to leave a personal legacy strikes me as one more piece of human hubris. Memories matter, but they do not need to be kept forever so that my ego is never forgotten. Ernest Becker called such efforts [immortality projects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denial_of_Death): ways of making our significance outlast our lives. It is fine if the universe forgets us.

I am a terrestrial [African ape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homininae), made by the universe and allowed, for a while, to see it. [The universe owes me nothing](personal-growth.md), so the right response is to notice what I was given and enjoy the damn moment.

That sounded too bleak to me once I had written about [beauty](../mind/beauty.md), and I think I see why. Two wishes hide in one word. Legacy is wanting my name to last, which is a way of winning. Posterity is wanting the good thing to last, with or without my name on it. Erik Erikson called that second wish [generativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generativity), a concern for the next generation.

To me it is the sense of beauty pointed forward. You plant the tree because a world with the tree in it is better, not because anyone will remember who planted it.

[Bertrand Russell](growing-old.md) answered the fear of death by letting the walls of the ego recede. The same cure works here. Drop the legacy. Keep the posterity. Then go back to the moment.

==== Mix Music Into a Video (Life) https://que.one/life/mix-music-video.html
Kind: howto

## Mix Music Into a Video

Put a song under a clip's own sound with [FFmpeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FFmpeg), so the room noise stays and the music plays over it. Start with the song as an audio file. If the song is inside a video, pull the audio out first.

### 1. Extract the song

```bash
ffmpeg -i song.mp4 -vn -c:a copy song.m4a
```

- `-vn`: drops the video stream.
- `-c:a copy`: copies the audio without re-encoding.

### 2. Trim the start of the song

```bash
ffmpeg -ss 15 -i song.m4a -c copy song-cut.m4a
```

- `-ss 15`: starts 15 seconds in. Placed before `-i`, it seeks the input, so the cut is fast.
- `-c copy`: copies the stream without re-encoding.

Repeat with a different offset until the song starts where the clip needs it.

### 3. Mix the song under the clip

```bash
ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 -i song-cut.m4a \
  -filter_complex "[0:a]volume=0.5[v];[1:a]volume=2.0[m];[v][m]amix=inputs=2:duration=first" \
  -c:v copy mixed.mp4
```

- `[0:a]volume=0.5[v]`: the clip's own audio at half volume, labeled `v`.
- `[1:a]volume=2.0[m]`: the song at double volume, labeled `m`.
- `amix=inputs=2:duration=first`: mixes the two and stops when the first input, the clip, ends.
- `-c:v copy`: keeps the video stream untouched, so only the audio is re-encoded.

`amix` scales each input down so the sum does not clip. The two volume filters set the balance before that scaling. Adjust the two numbers until the voices and the music sit right, then run step 3 again.

==== Personal Growth (Life) https://que.one/life/personal-growth.html
Kind: take

## Personal Growth

What I have settled on for [personal growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_development) fits in a few lines. Keep changing. The goal is to be a different and better person than I was ten years ago, not to defend that older version.

Start from one fact: neither the universe nor anyone in it owes me anything. That turns every good thing into something to notice, not something to expect. Good things do tend to happen to lucky people. But luck is partly built. I can put myself in the places, rooms, and habits where luck is more likely to find me.

Value the small things, without becoming obsessed with them, and never take them for granted. Joke most of the time, and save politics for talk that can be thoughtful and substantive. And outsource wisely. When a task is outside my skill or my time, and I can afford it, paying someone who does it well is not laziness. It is leverage. The older I get, the more that trade is worth.

Compressed into a mantra, it reads like this. [Keep life simple](../tech/ordenador.md). Accept reality. Improve my [models of the world](../mind/domain-specific-models.md) gradually, in myself and in others. Stand for compassion, progress, reason, and myself, and never surrender them.

==== Poker (Life) https://que.one/life/poker.html
Kind: reference

## Poker

Chip counts, blind schedules, and payouts I reuse for home games, with standard [poker chip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poker_chip) colors and a tournament [blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_%28poker%29) ladder. For a night out, see [Karaoke](karaoke.md).

- Cash game
```text
  $40 buy-in
  4  green/25c =   1.00
  8  blue/50c  =   4.00
  10 white/$1  =  10.00
  5  red/$5    =  25.00
  Total        = $40.00
```

- Tournament game
```text
  Each player gets $2000 in chips:
  4 green/$25   =   100
  8 blue/$50    =   400
  5 white/$100  =   500  (or 5 black/$100)
  2 purple/$500 =  1000  (or 1 yellow/$1000)
  Total         =  2000
  BLIND SCHEDULE
  LEVEL      SMALL     BIG
  Level 1      25       50
  Level 2      50      100
  Level 3     100      200
  Level 4     200      400
  Level 5     300      600
  Level 6     500    1,000
  Level 7   1,000    2,000
  Level 8   2,000    4,000
  Level 9   4,000    8,000
  Level 10  5,000   10,000
  SAMPLE PAYOUTS
  $40 buy-in
    6 Players
      Total = 240  1st=200  2nd=40
      Additional buy-ins are split between 1st & 2nd 4:1 ratio
    8 Players
      Total = 320  1st=200  2nd=80  3rd=40
      Additional buy-ins are split between 1st & 2nd 3:2 ratio
  $20 buy-in
    6 Players
      Total = 120  1st=100  2nd=20
      Additional buy-ins are split between 1st & 2nd 4:1 ratio
    8 Players
      Total = 160  1st=100  2nd=40  3rd=20
      Additional buy-ins are split between 1st & 2nd 3:2 ratio
```

==== Answer Patterns (Mind) https://que.one/mind/answer-patterns.html
Kind: note

## Answer Patterns

I sort answers along four lines. This helps me see what an answer is doing before I decide what it is worth.

- **Truth value.** Yes agrees. No denies. Don't know admits doubt. Maybe adds conditions.
- **Form.** A short answer is direct. A long answer explains or explores, and it usually carries some doubt with it.
- **Intent.** An answer can inform, persuade, entertain, or take responsibility for being right. Often it does two of these at once.
- **Certainty.** High goes with a clean Yes or No. Medium adds hedges. Low sits with Don't know or guessing.

The useful move is to read the intent first. "You should definitely try this" is a short, persuasive Yes with medium certainty. Knowing that tells me how much weight to give it.

==== Attention (Mind) https://que.one/mind/attention.html
Kind: reference

## Attention

Findings on attention from [Steven Pinker](pinker.md)'s introductory [psychology lectures](https://stevenpinker.com/psy-1-introduction-psychological-science-lectures). Other entries build on these.

### Two ways the mind processes

- **Parallel**: many things at once. The brain handles [incoming stimuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_processing_(psychology)) of different kinds at the same time, such as color, motion, shape, and depth.
- **Serial**: one thing at a time. Whatever needs focal attention goes through this bottleneck.

### Feature integration theory

[Anne Treisman and Garry Gelade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feature_integration_theory), 1980.

- Single features are registered "early, automatically, and in parallel".
- A target that differs by one feature [pops out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_search), however many distractors surround it. Think of a red dot among green ones.
- A target defined by a conjunction of features does not pop out. Wikipedia's example is a green X among purple Xs and green Os. Joining the features takes focal attention, which is serial, so the search slows as the crowd grows.

### Attention and awareness

- In the lectures, attention is a necessary condition for consciousness.
- [Inattentional blindness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inattentional_blindness) is the proof. In a famous study, people busy with a visual task failed to notice a person in a gorilla costume walking through the scene.

### The global workspace

[Bernard Baars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_workspace_theory), 1988.

- Consciousness works like a blackboard. Baars took the idea from early artificial-intelligence systems in which independent programs shared information on one.
- Only a small, relevant subset of information is posted.
- What is posted is shared among mid-level perception, language, memory, and planning.
- In the lectures, the brain side of this is connectivity to the frontal lobes.

What reaches the blackboard, and what never does, is covered under [Consciousness](consciousness.md).

==== Avoid and Practice (Mind) https://que.one/mind/avoid-and-practice.html
Kind: reference

## Avoid and Practice

Truth-seeking is a duty. Most entries on this site end in the same shape: stop doing one thing and start doing another. This page collects those pairs, one line each. The linked entry makes the case, and it wins wherever the two disagree.

### Talking with others

| Avoid | Practice | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Feeding identity politics | Truth-seeking dialogue that treats disagreement as information | [U.S. Identity Politics](../society/us-identity-politics.md), [Discourse](../society/discourse.md) |
| Arguing to win | Restate the other side so well they wish they had said it | [Discourse](../society/discourse.md) |
| Ridicule | Education, respect, and rapport | [Pseudoscience](pseudoscience.md) |
| Arguing someone out of a comforting belief | Norms, trusted messengers, and institutions | [Comfort and Biases](comfort-biases.md) |
| Attacking the person | Criticize the position | [Cold Logic](cold-logic.md), [Dunning-Kruger](dunning-kruger.md) |
| Bickering that scorns the listener | Disagree with civility, and say first what you agree on | [Smug Pilots](../society/smug-pilots.md) |
| Outrage and social punishment | Speed, simplicity, trusted messengers, and repetition | [Viral Truth](../society/viral-truth.md) |

### Thinking

| Avoid | Practice | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Collecting identity labels | Hold labels lightly and values firmly | [Hold Your Identity Lightly](identity-lightly.md) |
| Reaching for the familiar model | Ask first which model fits | [Domain-Specific Models](domain-specific-models.md) |
| Relying on willpower | Institutions and tools outside the head | [Two Systems](two-systems.md) |
| Grading your own paper | Welcome an honest review from someone who knows more | [Dunning-Kruger](dunning-kruger.md) |
| Taking a framing at face value | Ask who benefits from it | [Perception Management](../society/perception-management.md) |
| Believing a claim that needs many silent conspirators | Count the people who would have to keep the secret | [Detecting Baloney](detecting-baloney.md) |
| Judging a country by the people you know | Ask how big and how fair the sample is | [Detecting Baloney](detecting-baloney.md) |
| Staying deluded when facts are easy to check | Use AI and open data, and check the AI too | [Detecting Baloney](detecting-baloney.md) |
| Heavy partisan news | Cut back | [The Perception Gap](../society/perception-gap.md) |
| Discounting help because a machine gave it | Judge the writing by its claims | [Written With Help](../tech/written-with-help.md) |

### Public life

| Avoid | Practice | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Blaming one face | Change the rules | [Oligarchy](../society/oligarchy.md) |
| Treating markets as moral oracles | Judge them by their rules and incentives | [Markets and Capitalism](../society/markets-capitalism.md) |
| Handing a public problem to one donor | Public rules, and grading giving on what it fixed | [Whose Problem](../society/whose-problem.md) |
| Silence when the moment is consequential | Speak a little louder | [The Money Exception](../society/money-exception.md) |
| Purity tests | Coalitions with imperfect allies | [Activism](../society/activism.md) |
| Spending effort beyond your influence | Match effort to influence | [Activism](../society/activism.md) |
| Starting over each time | Build on each other's work | [Salomon's House](../society/salomons-house.md) |
| Keeping quiet once an argument convinced you | Say so openly, and build on the work | [After New Atheism](../society/after-new-atheism.md) |
| Closing the door behind you | Solidarity with those who opened it, and voting accordingly | [Who Opened the Door](../society/who-opened-the-door.md) |
| Easy reverence for the troops | Honor every profession that serves, and ask how troops are used | [Who We Thank](../society/who-we-thank.md) |
| Removing a workforce already here | A conditional path to legal status, with enforcement at the border | [The Immigration Choice](../society/immigration-choice.md) |
| Moral panics and purity tests | Equal rights, evidence, and free inquiry | [Trans Issues](../society/trans-issues.md) |

| Calling institutional decay strength | Judge by the Constitution, restraint, and the rule of law | [Not Conservatism](../society/not-conservatism.md) |
| Moral display without action | Ask what a stance cost, starting with your own | [Virtue Signaling](../society/virtue-signaling.md) |

|---|---|---|

==== Beauty (Mind) https://que.one/mind/beauty.html
Kind: note

## Beauty

Our sense of [beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty) strikes me as the most redeeming thing about us. We stop to look at a sunset that gives us nothing. Where that sense comes from is an open question, and the answers on offer disagree.

One answer is mate choice. Darwin argued in The Descent of Man that animals choose mates for their looks. [Richard Prum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Evolution_of_Beauty) has revived the idea as a force of its own in evolution.

A second answer is the useful signal. What looks good to us once helped us. Children from many nations [prefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_aesthetics) pictures of savanna with trees, the kind of landscape where much of human evolution is thought to have happened.

A third is the by-product. [Steven Pinker](pinker.md) called music "[auditory cheesecake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_musicology)". A taste for fat and sugar was useful. Cheesecake played no part in that selection. It just presses the buttons.

A fourth says beauty is real. The physicist [David Deutsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Deutsch) argues that there is [objective beauty](https://www.nature.com/articles/526S16a). Some beauty is local to a species or a culture, he says, and some is universal, "[as objective as the laws of physics](https://www.onfiction.ca/2012/04/david-deutsch-on-objective-beauty.html)". His case is the flower, which evolved to attract insects and yet attracts us.

I lean toward the by-product, and I get there from the body. Pleasure is the useful signal. Eating when hungry feels good, and so, to be plain, does relieving yourself. What helps the body feels right. My guess is that the sense of beauty is that same machinery. It fires at things it was never built for: a sunset, a fugue, an equation.

Brain scans fit this. One region [responds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroesthetics) to beauty in paintings, in music, and even in mathematics.

Pleasure and beauty are still not the same thing. [Kant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critique_of_Judgment) drew the line long ago. The agreeable is a good steak. The beautiful is something we stop to contemplate, wanting nothing from it.

So I part with Deutsch on one point. He thinks the standard is out there. I think it is in us, a by-product that works as a compass. It draws us to objects and ideas that sit in harmony with what we are. That is why I call it redeeming. It is a way of choosing that has [nothing to do with winning](../life/legacy.md).

[Science](science.md) tells me what is true. Beauty helps me choose what is worth wanting.

==== Noam Chomsky (Mind) https://que.one/mind/chomsky.html
Kind: note

## Noam Chomsky

[Noam Chomsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noam_Chomsky) is the thinker who did the most to shape how I see the world. A magazine profile led me to him early on. I had never met a more honest or more scientific view of reality.

He has two sides: the cognitive scientist and the political dissident. On thinking and morality I agree with him on almost everything. In politics he has made the world better by standing with the oppressed. Many people find his positions hard to put into practice, and I tend to agree.

Following my inner [Popper](popper.md), the place where I differ is more interesting than the agreements. Chomsky holds that language appeared through a single mutation, not through slow selection. This is his [single-step theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_of_language#Chomsky's_single-step_theory). That treats one human trait as special, almost magical. I find the gradual account that [Dennett](dennett.md) defends more likely.

### Limits to human intelligence

> If there were no limits to human intelligence, it would lack internal structure and would therefore have no scope. — Noam Chomsky, [Science, Mind, and Limits of Understanding](https://chomsky.info/201401__/)

His point, from that essay and from an [interview](https://youtu.be/XSgUCMkt8us) with [Lex Fridman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Fridman), is simple. A living system can only build and organize information within limits. Those limits are the structure that makes thinking possible.

Dennett pushed back. Limits need not be inborn, since structure can grow from learning, environment, and evolution. Intelligence is what a system reliably does, not a fixed set of rules. A tool that extends the mind would add to our limits, not remove them. Even an artificial general intelligence built on other principles would leave Chomsky's point standing for human minds.

==== Cold Logic (Mind) https://que.one/mind/cold-logic.html
Kind: take

## Cold Logic

Cold logic is my name for reasoning that follows a rule past the point where it stops helping people. It is firm, consistent, and blind to feeling, flaw, and circumstance. It turns lives into numbers and treats efficiency as the only virtue. It is tempting because it looks airtight on paper.

The idea is not new. [J. J. C. Smart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._C._Smart) called following a rule, even when breaking it would be better, "superstitious rule worship". [Max Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumental_and_value-rational_action) separated reasoning about means from reasoning about ends. The [eugenics movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compulsory_sterilization) is the clearest case. Sterilization programs were sold as improvement, and the suffering they caused was left out of the sum.

The opposite failure is real too. Warm sentiment, meaning choices made purely from feeling, brings its own chaos and harm. I see the two as ends of one scale. Lean cold for safety and technical choices, where feeling clouds judgment. Lean warm for relationships and community, where compassion is the point. And remember that even the most rational system has to stay tied to the people it governs.

For public figures, cold logic describes a position, never a person. That is how [libertarianism](../society/libertarianism.md) is handled on this site.

==== Comfort and Biases (Mind) https://que.one/mind/comfort-biases.html
Kind: note

## Comfort and Biases

Some people show little wish to understand the world as it is. They live inside belief systems that are cut off from reality but make a messy life feel manageable. The systems last not because they are true but because they bring stability and certainty. It is tempting, and I have been tempted, to call that an empty mind. It is better seen as a set of well-known mechanisms.

Beliefs often work as tools for calming feelings and for belonging, not as [models of reality](domain-specific-models.md). [Steven Pinker](pinker.md) names the split in his book [Rationality](https://newhumanist.org.uk/articles/for-the-love-of-reason/). The reality mindset covers what we must get right: nobody doubts that a car needs gas. The mythology mindset covers the far away and the unprovable, where beliefs serve morals, identity, and fun.

So evidence gets filtered by whether it threatens balance or standing. Deep understanding is costly. Most of us save effort by adopting ready-made systems, whether political, religious, or conspiratorial, that give order cheaply. Once inside, people pick what they see and distrust outside experts, and the exits close. Some people simply have practical curiosity rather than a need to explain things. And leaving a worldview can feel like dying, since it carries meaning, identity, and community with it.

From an evolutionary view all of this is useful. Truth was never evolution's priority. Stability was.

### The Ultimate Bias

None of this applies only to other people. [Aileen Oeberst and Roland Imhoff](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/17456916221148147) argue that most familiar biases grow from a few basic beliefs. Two examples are "I make good judgments" and "I am a good person." One ultimate bias holds them up: [confirmation bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confirmation_bias). That is the [reflexivity limitation](reflexivity.md#the-reflexivity-limitation) at work. A brain cannot fully watch its own reasoning, so it favors what it already holds.

The difference between people is not freedom from bias. It is the will to notice and correct it. Pause before accepting a claim. Seek people who think differently. Look for evidence that would prove you wrong. Notice when a belief feels good.

Those habits have limits, because they depend on a reflexivity that not everyone has to the same degree. That is why outside supports matter more than willpower, the subject of [augmenting reflexivity](reflexivity.md#augmenting-our-reflexivity). It is also why arguing someone out of a comforting belief rarely works. Norms, trusted messengers, and institutions do, as [cultural cognition](cultural-cognition.md) explains.

==== Complexity (Mind) https://que.one/mind/complexity.html
Kind: reference

## Complexity

Terms for talking about complexity, with how settled each one is. Other entries build on these.

### Two fields share one word

- **Computational complexity** sorts problems by the time and memory it takes to solve them. Its best-known open question is [P versus NP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P_versus_NP_problem). The field is [settled mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory) with famous unsolved problems.
- **Complex systems** studies many interacting parts that produce behavior none of them has alone. It is an [interdisciplinary field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_system) that borrows tools from physics, biology, mathematics, and the social sciences, not a single theory. The [Santa Fe Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe_Institute) is its best-known home.

Popular writing slides between the two. Check which one a claim means.

### Terms

| Term | Plain meaning | How settled | On this site |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Emergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergence) | A whole has properties its parts lack on their own. | Established as a description | [The Ouroboros](ouroboros.md) |
| [Self-organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-organization) | Order arises from local interactions, with no one in charge. | Established | |
| [Complex adaptive system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_adaptive_system) | A network of parts whose whole cannot be predicted from the parts, and which adapts. | Established framework | [Four Floors](four-floors.md) |
| [Chaos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaos_theory) | Exact rules, but so sensitive to starting conditions that the future cannot be predicted in practice. | Established mathematics | |
| [Edge of chaos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_of_chaos) | A zone between order and disorder where adaptive complexity may arise. | Hypothesis | [The Ouroboros](ouroboros.md) |
| [Self-organized criticality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-organized_criticality) | A system that tunes itself to a tipping point, like a sandpile that slides in avalanches. | Established model, debated reach | |
| [Power law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_law) | A heavy-tailed pattern in which rare huge events dominate. | Established mathematics, often misclaimed | |
| [Network science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science) | The study of nodes and links, from the internet to brains. | Established | |
| Computational irreducibility | Some outcomes cannot be predicted faster than by running them. | A widely cited framing | [Computation](computation.md) |
| Assembly theory | Measures a thing by the fewest steps it takes to build. | Young, contested | [The Ouroboros](ouroboros.md) |
| Functional information | Grows when selection favors what a system does. | A proposed law | [The Ouroboros](ouroboros.md) |

### Common traps

- **Calling anything complicated emergent.** Emergence names properties the parts lack, not complication.
- **Reading chaos as disorder.** Chaotic systems follow exact rules. They are unpredictable, not random.
- **Seeing a power law in any straight line on a log plot.** [Clauset, Shalizi, and Newman](https://arxiv.org/abs/0706.1062) tested published claims and found the power law ruled out in some cases. The usual least-squares fit gives inaccurate estimates.
- **Mixing the two fields.** A problem that is hard to compute is not a complex system.
- **Using the word as an explanation.** "Complexity" can do what "quantum" does in pseudoscience: sound like a reason without being one. [Detecting Baloney](detecting-baloney.md) has the checks.

==== Computation (Mind) https://que.one/mind/computation.html
Kind: take

## Computation

[Stephen Wolfram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Wolfram), among others, points out that we used to treat computing problems as separate things. Sorting a list, taking a square root, and checking whether a phrase is a palindrome looked like three different tasks. Since [Kurt Gödel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_G%C3%B6del) and [Alan Turing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing) we know they are the same kind of problem. They are all cases of universal computation. I find that shift in view still worth pausing on.

One tempting conclusion is that we can compute anything with the newest models and enough machines. Wolfram's [computational irreducibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_irreducibility) says that is wrong. For much complex behavior there is no shortcut theory. You cannot predict the result. The program must still be run to get an answer.

I wonder how much of that was already implied by complexity theory, by [Gödel's incompleteness theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del%27s_incompleteness_theorems), and by the [halting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halting_problem). Those ideas are almost a century old.

Caring about computation matters because it leads to big shifts in how we see things. [Copernicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus) moving us away from the center of the universe is the famous example. Before and after him, computing planet positions with [Ptolemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy)'s epicycles worked well enough for most uses. It was only less accurate. More accuracy in our understanding is what such a shift buys.

==== Consciousness (Mind) https://que.one/mind/consciousness.html
Kind: note

## Consciousness

[Steven Pinker](pinker.md)'s introductory [psychology lectures](https://stevenpinker.com/psy-1-introduction-psychological-science-lectures) split consciousness the way the philosopher David Chalmers did, into easy problems and a [hard problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_problem_of_consciousness).

The easy problem is access. Some information is available to us: the objects we see, our plans, the content of a sentence. Some is not: the rules of syntax, the image on the retina, the commands to our muscles.

"Easy" is an in-joke. It is still very hard, but science has a way in. [Attention](attention.md) decides what gets through. The leading account is a [global workspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_workspace_theory), a blackboard where a small, relevant subset of information is posted for memory, language, and planning to share.

The hard problem is sentience: why any of this feels like something. Philosophers call the raw feels [qualia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qualia), such as the painfulness of pain or the smell of cinnamon. Is your blue my blue? Could a program feel? Could there be a [zombie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophical_zombie) that acts like us with nobody home?

The lectures list the answers on offer. Dualism leaves too many open questions. Information-processing theories cannot say why a flow of bits should feel like anything, and they slide toward [panpsychism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panpsychism), with conscious thermostats. Neural theories point to brain rhythms, and [Penrose](penrose.md) points to quantum gravity, and both still owe us the how. The [mysterians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_mysterianism) say our brains may lack the means to solve it. And [Daniel Dennett](dennett.md) says there is no hard problem: sentience, as something over and above the machinery, is an illusion.

I side with Dennett. I expect consciousness to get a materialist explanation in the end. Life itself looked like this kind of mystery in the nineteenth century, and it turned out to be molecules, organized by natural selection. Descartes's objection, that I cannot be wrong about my own experience, does not move me.

That does not make the mysterians wrong about today. [Chomsky's limits](chomsky.md) on human understanding are real, I think, for the brain as it now is. They hold until we find a way to augment it, which may or may never happen.

==== Human Core Challenges (Mind) https://que.one/mind/core-challenges.html
Kind: note

## Human Core Challenges

Three problems sit under every other problem humanity has. I find them largely invisible at first glance.

The **biological problem** is that our genes strongly shape our behavior. Twin studies in [behavioural genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behavioural_genetics) put the heritability of most behavioral traits near half. [Evolutionary psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_psychology) has been showing why for decades, though society is still catching up. Knowing this makes it easier to accept ourselves and others. It also makes it unreasonable to expect people to change their minds easily.

Some brains are wired like a program that returns one result. We also carry a built-in [list of cognitive biases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cognitive_biases). The strongest is confirmation bias, which I treat as [the ultimate bias](comfort-biases.md#the-ultimate-bias), and the deeper limit I call the [reflexivity limitation](reflexivity.md#the-reflexivity-limitation). Progress is still possible, only slow.

The **social problem** is the set of imperfect institutions that grow out of those biological limits. [Edward O. Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._O._Wilson) put it best in a debate recorded on [Wikiquote](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/E._O._Wilson): "we have paleolithic emotions; medieval institutions; and god-like technology." Technology, at least, is a good outgrowth of our biology. History shows the social problem gives way. Advanced nations have built fairly stable societies. That is a long way from the "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short" default that [Thomas Hobbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes) described.

The **entropy problem** is the least acknowledged. Its formal statement, the [second law of thermodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_law_of_thermodynamics), sounds abstract. So I prefer the memory aid from [Steven Pinker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlightenment_Now): things fall apart. Bodies, societies, and the planet decay without care and upkeep. Life is a constant struggle to survive and to flourish.

The essential question for our species is this. Is progress limited to the slow change we have seen, or can solutions be sped up?

==== Cultural Cognition (Mind) https://que.one/mind/cultural-cognition.html
Kind: take

## Cultural Cognition

[Cultural cognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_cognition) is the habit of reading facts and evidence in whatever way fits the values and groups you already belong to. It is common, but it is neither universal nor certain. Psychological tendencies describe common patterns, not laws. People with moderate views, strong habits of honesty, or plain awareness of the bias resist it or partly correct for it. Treating the tendency as fate goes too far, and I keep that exception in view.

For one person, the move is to [hold your identity lightly](identity-lightly.md). The practical question is how a society moves past identity-driven thinking. The answer is not better arguments. Lasting change comes from removing the signals that trigger partisan defense. It also comes from messengers trusted across group lines: scientists, community leaders, and peers who can speak without taking a side.

A large middle does not read the world through a political lens at all. Institutions and media should give it more voice by rewarding nuance over outrage. The shifts in public views on smoking, same-sex marriage, and sexual harassment show the pattern. Evidence took hold once social norms, trusted messengers, and institutions backed it. That is also why arguing someone out of a comforting belief rarely works, as [Comfort and Biases](comfort-biases.md) and [Pseudoscience](pseudoscience.md) describe. Norms and institutions do.

==== Richard Dawkins (Mind) https://que.one/mind/dawkins.html
Kind: take

## Richard Dawkins

[Richard Dawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dawkins) did not invent the gene's-eye view of evolution. [W. D. Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._D._Hamilton) and [George C. Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_C._Williams_(biologist)) worked it out in the 1960s, and [John Maynard Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Maynard_Smith) gave it game theory. What Dawkins did in [The Selfish Gene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Selfish_Gene) (1976) was make it the common frame. Selection acts on [replicators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene-centered_view_of_evolution), the genes. Bodies are the vehicles genes build to copy themselves.

The gene's-eye view settles what an adaptation is for. It serves the replication of the genes that build it, not the individual, the group, or the species. Once that is settled, the mind looks like a set of adaptations with jobs to do. That footing is what evolutionary psychology stands on, and it is why the mental programs of [John Tooby](tooby.md) make sense as programs. [Daniel Dennett](dennett.md) draws out what the same idea does to meaning and design.

I also read him for how he writes. His prose is poetic, rare in science, and still compellingly rational, with no lovely sentence carrying an argument the evidence will not. [Unweaving the Rainbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unweaving_the_Rainbow) is his answer to the charge that explaining a thing kills its wonder, and the book is its own evidence.

He is also one of the Four Horsemen, and [After New Atheism](../society/after-new-atheism.md) says what I think that argument achieved.

==== Daniel Dennett (Mind) https://que.one/mind/dennett.html
Kind: take

## Daniel Dennett

[Daniel Dennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Dennett) is the philosopher I keep returning to.

He died on April 19, 2024. That is the same calendar day [Charles Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin) died in 1882, which the universe surely meant as a nod.

He was the philosopher who respected science and engineering. I loved his [intuition pumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuition_pump) for thinking clearly, and I keep [one of my own](threads-of-mind.md). I side with him on [consciousness](consciousness.md) too. A line attributed to him says that one surprising discovery of modern psychology is how easy it is to be ignorant of your own ignorance. That is what I call low [reflexivity](reflexivity.md).

In [Darwin's Dangerous Idea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darwin%27s_Dangerous_Idea) he argues that natural selection joined two worlds. One is the world of mechanism and matter. The other is the world of meaning and purpose. Until Darwin the two looked impossible to bridge, and Dennett calls Darwin's idea perhaps the greatest anyone ever had. At this point in history I think he was right.

The same slow, step-by-step view dissolves the mind-body problem. The unified self is a marvelous evolved illusion. There is no little person at the center of consciousness. And nothing about calculation is "mere", since it was only ever a matter of scale and complexity.

Deep emotional attachment is what life is about. Nurturing it is what brings happiness, the closest thing we have to a highest good. His attributed advice is the one I keep: find something more important than you are and dedicate your life to it.

==== Desire (Mind) https://que.one/mind/desire.html
Kind: note

## Desire

I find it useful to put wanting on one scale that runs from hatred to addiction. The same thing can sit anywhere on it depending on the day. The label tells me how much the feeling should be trusted.

| # | Feeling | Level | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hatred | -5 | An extreme aversion, often driven by anger or fear. |
| 2 | Aversion | -3 | A strong dislike or unwillingness toward something. |
| 3 | Disinterest | -1 | Lack of interest or motivation. |
| 4 | Neutral | 0 | Neither desire nor aversion; a balanced state. |
| 5 | Simple wish | 1 | A minor want or preference that is easily fulfilled. |
| 6 | Moderate desire | 3 | A meaningful but balanced motivation to reach a goal. |
| 7 | Fixation | 4 | A focused desire that dominates attention but fits the context. |
| 8 | Obsession | 5 | An intrusive, persistent desire that can cause distress. |
| 9 | Addiction | 5 | An uncontrollable desire, often with negative consequences. |

The scale runs separately in each of my [three realms](three-realms.md): the physical, the emotional, and the intellectual. For the wider vocabulary, see [Emotions and Relational States](emotions.md).

==== Detecting Baloney (Mind) https://que.one/mind/detecting-baloney.html
Kind: note

## Detecting Baloney

Baloney is foolish, senseless, or absurd words and ideas. Spotting it belongs in everyone's kit for defending their own mind. My pointers:

- Read and listen to the late [Carl Sagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sagan) and to [Michael Shermer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Shermer).
- Start with Sagan's baloney detection kit from [The Demon-Haunted World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Demon-Haunted_World). It is summarized at [The Mind Collection](https://themindcollection.com/baloney-detection-kit/).
- Two good clips: [Shermer, clip one](https://youtu.be/mn7jVTGjb-I) and [Shermer, clip two](https://youtu.be/aNSHZG9blQQ).
- Be careful with [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=baloney+detection+kit) and with social media feeds in general. Depending on the topic, they are built to stir feelings.
- Build your own list of trusted sources. Do not rely on whatever the feed serves.
- Check a claim against several credible outlets before you accept it.
- Use the tools. AI and open data make checking a basic fact quick, as long as you [check the AI](../tech/written-with-help.md) too. Staying deluded about basic realities is a refusal to engage, not a lack of means.
- Count the people who would have to keep the secret. Many conspiracy theories assume that hundreds of ordinary people can keep a secret for years. Most of us struggle to keep one for a weekend. Shermer's [conspiracy detector](https://michaelshermer.com/sciam-columns/the-conspiracy-theory-detector/) says: "The more people involved, the less realistic it becomes." A [2016 model](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0147905) by David Robert Grimes found that conspiracies of a thousand people or more "quickly become untenable and prone to failure".
- Ask how big and how fair the sample is. The ten or fifteen people you know are not the country. Nobody has to visit every pizzeria to estimate how much pizza Americans eat, because a fair [sample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_(statistics)) gives the answer with high confidence.

==== Domain-Specific Models (Mind) https://que.one/mind/domain-specific-models.html
Kind: note

## Domain-Specific Models

I find it useful to see a person's belief system as a system of domain-specific models. Each of us builds them unnoticed over years to survive and thrive: one for money, one for work, one for strangers, one for illness. Each is a set of [rules of thumb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heuristic_(psychology)).

The models differ. Some are simple and some complex. Some run all day, some hardly ever.

Accuracy matters less than we think. A model survives if it satisfies its owner's passions and seems to get results. Herbert Simon called that [satisficing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satisficing): stopping at good enough. [Gerd Gigerenzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecological_rationality) adds that a rule of thumb works when it fits the setting it grew up in. Move it to another setting and it fails.

Psychology has older names for the parts. George Kelly held in the 1950s that every person is [a scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_construct_theory), building models of how the world works. My label borrows from cognitive science, where [domain specificity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_specificity) means the mind comes with specialized, inborn learning devices, a view [Pinker](pinker.md) and [Chomsky](chomsky.md) hold. The models start from [inborn parts](tooby.md), and a lifetime of learning shapes them.

Two things make a model hard to change. It sticks to identity like velcro, which is the ground [cultural cognition](cultural-cognition.md) covers. And it [comforts](comfort-biases.md). Few of us step outside the pull of our own.

The worst models are often installed in childhood, like shame about [sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purity_culture) or a [politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_socialization) of enemies. Parents who mean no harm pass on what their values require, a cause of [unintended consequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unintended_consequences) Robert Merton named. The carrier is more often a victim of the process than wicked.

The common failure is misapplication. A rigid mind reaches for the model it knows and uses it on the wrong problem. Psychologists call this the [Einstellung effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstellung_effect): solving a problem the familiar way even though a better way exists. It is the old line about the hammer and the nail, the [law of the instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_instrument). A flexible mind asks first which model fits.

The way out is [reflexivity](reflexivity.md), seeing a model as a model. I do not think this sorts people into two kinds. Everyone has sealed models in some domains, and I have mine. [The less I know a field](dunning-kruger.md), the less likely I am to notice. The work is gradual: find one sealed model, test it against the world, and repair it. Then help someone else do the same.

==== Dunning-Kruger (Mind) https://que.one/mind/dunning-kruger.html
Kind: note

## Dunning-Kruger

One of the best clips I know about how hard it is to hear that you are wrong runs 17 minutes.

In 2024 the actor [Terrence Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrence_Howard) told [Joe Rogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Joe_Rogan_Experience)'s audience that [Neil deGrasse Tyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_deGrasse_Tyson) had ["attacked"](https://www.blackenterprise.com/neil-degrasse-tyson-terrence-howard-attacking-scientific-findings/) his treatise. It argues that one times one equals two. Tyson's [reply](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1uLi1I3G2N4) shows what happened eight years earlier. He had read all 36 pages and marked them up in red.

"In my field we call that a [peer review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer_review)," he says. His notes open by calling the work the sign of "a restless, active mind". Then they list what is "under-informed, misinformed, or simply false". He was blunt, he wrote, out of respect for the effort.

Tyson then names the trap. You can know enough about a subject to think you are right, but not enough to know you are wrong. "It's called the [Dunning–Kruger effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunning%E2%80%93Kruger_effect)."

Is the effect real? Partly. In the [1999 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10626367/), students who scored in the 12th percentile placed themselves in the 62nd. That gap keeps turning up.

But the popular version, that the ignorant feel like experts, is not what was found. The weakest students still rated themselves below the strongest. The finding is about one skill at a time, not about intelligence.

The cause is disputed too. [Critics](https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/critical-thinking/dunning-kruger-effect-probably-not-real) have shown that random numbers produce the same chart. Two ordinary things do it: [regression toward the mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_toward_the_mean), and the habit most of us have of rating ourselves [above average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusory_superiority). [David Dunning](https://www.bps.org.uk/psychologist/dunning-kruger-effect-and-its-discontents) answered in 2022 that the effect survives when both are controlled for.

I draw two lessons. First, I try not to hang the label on a person. The finding covers all of us outside our own field, and [those who most need to reflect are the least open to it](reflexivity.md). On most subjects that includes me. It is fair to say that one times one is not two. It is not fair to diagnose the man who says it.

Second, the remedy does not wait on the statistics. Nobody can grade their own paper. An honest review from someone who knows more is a gift, even in red ink, and [respect, not ridicule](pseudoscience.md), is how Tyson delivered it. He closes with a saying he credits to Michael Dell: if you find yourself the smartest person in the room, change rooms.

==== Edge Website (Mind) https://que.one/mind/edge-website.html
Kind: take

## Edge Website

It looks silly when people brag about how much they know. Showing off knowledge makes humans look like street performers. But when people who know a lot get together and talk casually about what we know, that is a fine thing. That is what [Edge](https://www.edge.org) was: the smartest, most insightful salon on the web, and I still think it is worth a visit now and then.

As of 2023 the site had gone quiet.

The trouble is its founder. [John Brockman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Brockman_(literary_agent)) was closely tied to Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted sex offender. That does not erase the conversations. But it changes how I read the guest list.

==== Emotions and Relational States (Mind) https://que.one/mind/emotions.html
Kind: reference

## Emotions and Relational States

A vocabulary for feelings, and for the states that hold between people, kept for other entries to point to. Feelings come in degrees, so the first table is a set of scales. The grouping in the second and third parts is my own. For the published models, including Paul Ekman's six basic emotions and a Berkeley study's 27 categories, see [emotion classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification).

### Emotions by intensity

[Robert Plutchik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Plutchik) named eight primary emotions. "Like colors, primary emotions can be expressed at different intensities." Read the rows in pairs: each emotion is followed by its opposite.

| Mild | Basic | Intense |
|---|---|---|
| Serenity | Joy | Ecstasy |
| Pensiveness | Sadness | Grief |
| Acceptance | Trust | Admiration |
| Boredom | Disgust | Loathing |
| Apprehension | Fear | Terror |
| Annoyance | Anger | Rage |
| Distraction | Surprise | Amazement |
| Interest | Anticipation | Vigilance |

Desire has a scale of its own, under [Desire](desire.md).

### Other emotions

| Group | Emotions |
|---|---|
| Positive / Affectionate | Affection, love, respect, gratitude, fondness |
| Positive / Self-Oriented | Happiness, contentment, pride, relief, hope, confidence |
| Neutral / Complex | Indifference, curiosity, ambivalence, attachment |
| Motivational / Drive-Based | Frustration, longing |
| Arousal / Surprise-Based | Shock, confusion |
| Negative / Self-Oriented | Loneliness, anxiety, despair, helplessness, insecurity |
| Negative / Tense | Resentment, jealousy, envy, contempt, hatred, distrust, suspicion |
| Moral / Social | Pity, compassion, guilt, shame, forgiveness, disappointment |
| Power / Status-Related | Humiliation, status pride |
| Existential / Meaning-Based | Meaningfulness, emptiness, awe, existential fear, transcendence |

### Relational states

These are not emotions in the narrow sense. They are drives, or states that hold between people, and feelings travel with them.

| Group | States |
|---|---|
| Positive / Affectionate | Loyalty |
| Neutral / Complex | Dependence, obligation, familiarity |
| Motivational / Drive-Based | Ambition, determination, motivation |
| Power / Status-Related | Dominance, submission, empowerment |
| Interpersonal Boundary | Closeness, distance, rejection, inclusion, alienation |

==== Famous Lessons (Mind) https://que.one/mind/famous-lessons.html
Kind: reference

## Famous Lessons

A handy list of time-tested ideas and smart shortcuts for thinking.

## Occam’s Razor
When presented with competing explanations, the simplest one is usually best ([Occam’s Razor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occam%27s_razor)). This principle encourages cutting away unnecessary complexity and assumptions before forming judgments or taking action. The core lesson is **simplicity over needless complication**.  

## Hanlon’s Razor
Never attribute to malice that which can be explained by ignorance or error ([Hanlon’s Razor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanlon%27s_razor)). The idea is to assume mistakes or misunderstandings before jumping to ill intent. In critical thinking, it’s a reminder to **consider simpler explanations first** rather than imagining hidden agendas.  

## Chesterton’s Fence
Do not remove a rule, practice, or institution until you understand why it exists ([Chesterton’s Fence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chesterton%27s_fence)). It’s a warning to **understand before dismantling**.  

## Principle of Charity
In thinking and debating, try to understand and even strengthen an argument before you critique it ([Principle of Charity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_charity)). This is often called “steelmanning”: before pointing out flaws, make sure you’ve represented the argument in its strongest form. It’s closely related to Chesterton’s Fence, but applied to ideas rather than institutions. Philosophers also talk about “hermeneutic respect,” which is just a fancy way of saying: **understand before judging**.  

## Bulverism
Bulverism is the mistake of assuming something is wrong and attacking it without really examining it ([Bulverism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulverism)). It’s the opposite of the Principle of Charity and serves as a caution: **don’t condemn before understanding**. Like Chesterton’s Fence, it emphasizes the need for comprehension before criticism.  

## Sunk Cost Fallacy Reminder
Don’t continue investing in something just because you’ve already spent time, money, or effort ([Sunk Cost Fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunk_cost)). This principle warns against letting past investments cloud rational evaluation. The key takeaway is **decisions should be based on future value, not past costs**.  

## Sturgeon’s Law
Ninety percent of everything is mediocre or low quality ([Sturgeon’s Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturgeon%27s_law)). It’s a cheeky caution to **look past the noise** and focus on what is genuinely worthwhile, avoiding snap judgments based on quantity over quality.  

## The Map Is Not the Territory
Models, rules, and frameworks are simplifications of reality, not reality itself ([The Map Is Not the Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_map_is_not_the_territory)). This principle reminds you to **understand the real system** before acting, rather than blindly following abstractions.  


## Hume’s Guillotine
A claim about what is cannot by itself prove a claim about what ought to be ([Hume’s Guillotine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%E2%80%93ought_problem)). David Hume raised the point in 1739. A descriptive claim says how things are. A normative claim says what we should do.

The error runs both ways. “It is natural, so it is right” is the [appeal to nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appeal_to_nature). “It would be bad if it were true, so it is false” is the [moralistic fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moralistic_fallacy). The takeaway is **check which kind of claim you are reading before you argue with it**.

==== Famous Quotes (Mind) https://que.one/mind/famous-quotes.html
Kind: quote

## Famous Quotes

Quotes are useful cognitive anchors: a good line compresses a lesson into something memorable. The cost is that compression removes context, so I use them as prompts for reflection, never as substitutes for reasoning. Treat a quote as a pointer to an idea, not proof of it; ask what problem the line helps you notice or remember; and be wary of dramatic lines, whose emotional punch usually outruns their explanatory value. A few worth remembering, with my own English renderings:

### [Jorge Luis Borges](https://es.wikiquote.org/wiki/Jorge_Luis_Borges)

> Yo no hablo de venganzas ni de perdones; el olvido es la única venganza y el único perdón.

"I do not speak of revenge or forgiveness; forgetting is the only revenge and the only forgiveness." It is verse 27 of his 1969 poem [Fragmentos de un evangelio apócrifo](https://borgestodoelanio.blogspot.com/2014/09/jorge-luis-borges-fragmentos-de-un.html). It shifts attention from theatrical payback to release.

### [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Exit)

> L'enfer, c'est les autres.

"Hell is other people," from his 1944 play No Exit. It is repeated too casually. In a [1965 recorded preface](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huis_clos_(Sartre)) Sartre said the line had always been misunderstood: others become hell when our relations with them are twisted, because we depend on their judgment to know ourselves. The value is in remembering how social judgment, [status anxiety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Status_anxiety), and mutual dependence can become oppressive.

### [Spanish proverb](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Spanish_proverbs)

> No hay plazo que no se cumpla ni deuda que no se pague.

"Every deadline arrives, and every debt is paid." It is also the title of [Antonio de Zamora's 1722](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Juan) Don Juan play. Delay does not erase consequences.

### [Jean Cocteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Cocteau)

> Never associate with idiots on their own level, because … on their level they'll beat you every time.

Yul Brynner attributed it to his friend Cocteau in 1956. It is often [misattributed](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2023/01/29/never-argue/) to Mark Twain.

==== Four Floors (Mind) https://que.one/mind/four-floors.html
Kind: note

## Four Floors

I find it useful to trace motivation to four sources, each built on the one below. Daniel Dennett's [Tower of Generate-and-Test](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/finding-purpose/202509/where-do-cognition-and-consciousness-begin) names the first three floors. The fourth is mine.

The ground floor is genes. They interact inside the body and set the drives we start with. That is the [biological problem](core-challenges.md): heritability near half for most behavioral traits. [Tooby](tooby.md) calls the results evolved mental programs, and the [seeking system](transcendence.md) is one of them. Dennett calls a creature that runs on this floor alone Darwinian.

The second floor is reflection on what the genes produce. I fold in learning from reward here, which [Dennett](dennett.md) gives a floor of its own and calls Skinnerian. His Popperian creature goes further. It simulates an action in its head and anticipates the outcome before risking it in the world.

The third floor is other minds. Everyone we meet runs the first two floors too, and we borrow their words, tools, and habits. Dennett calls this creature Gregorian, after the psychologist [Richard Gregory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Gregory). [Cultural cognition](cultural-cognition.md) is this floor at work.

The fourth floor is reflection on the other three: noticing which drive, which lesson, and which borrowed idea is doing the pushing. That is [reflexivity](reflexivity.md). Dennett's tower folds it into the Gregorian floor, since language is what makes it possible. I keep it separate because it is the floor people climb least.

Ideology is what the floors build when they fuse. Belief, reason, and desire bind into one [bundle](domain-specific-models.md) that feels like plain truth from inside. Politics shows it well. Genes tilt the temperament, the second floor writes the story, the third supplies the tribe, and only the fourth can take the bundle apart.

==== Free Will (Mind) https://que.one/mind/free-will.html
Kind: note

## Free Will

[Free will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_will) is the old question of whether we truly choose. Can we pick among options, control our behavior, and start actions, rather than just be pushed by earlier causes? [Sam Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Harris) argued in [Free Will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Will_(book)) that it is an illusion. Decisions, he says, are fully caused by brain processes and background factors outside conscious control.

[Daniel Dennett](dennett.md), the leading defender of [compatibilism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compatibilism), answered in a [review](https://www.naturalism.org/resources/book-reviews/reflections-on-free-will). Free will, he said, means control, responding to reasons, and self-regulation, not a power that escapes cause and effect. Harris [replied](https://www.samharris.org/blog/the-marionettes-lament) that this changes the subject and dodges the question of ultimate authorship. I keep coming back to this exchange.

I found the tone of [Dennett's side](https://www.naturalism.org/resources/book-reviews/reflections-on-free-will) disappointing. It is one reason the [Discourse Protocol](../society/discourse.md) exists. Disagreement is certain, and progress depends on how it is handled.

On the substance, three layers help. The metaphysical question is whether choices are fixed by earlier states, including brain events. The psychological question is how deliberation actually happens. The normative question is whether people whose choices are caused should still be held accountable.

Much of the debate turns on [Benjamin Libet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Libet)'s experiments. There, a readiness signal in the brain comes before a voluntary act. Harris reads that as decisions being made before we know it. Later modeling by Aaron Schurger and colleagues, summarized under the [neuroscience of free will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroscience_of_free_will), shows the signal is not necessarily the cause. Dennett adds that the conscious author of an act needs no access to how the brain produces it. A sailor steers without controlling wind or current.

The real split is about degrees. Dennett treats freedom as more or less control. Harris treats it as all or nothing and [concludes](https://www.samharris.org/blog/the-marionettes-lament) that no one controls anything. One side means the ability to do otherwise under identical conditions. The other means being guided by one's own reasons. Positions that fit together then look opposed.

Defining terms, and separating the empirical from the conceptual, dissolves much of the fight. That matters because responsibility, law, and how we see ourselves all rest on it. My open question: is the demand for ultimate authorship a fair requirement or a mistake about concepts?

==== Holographic Space (Mind) https://que.one/mind/holographic-space.html
Kind: note

## Holographic Space

I see one world built in levels, from particles to minds, as [The Ouroboros](ouroboros.md) lays out. Space has always looked like the floor under those levels. Physics now hints that space may be a level too, and I find that fascinating.

The first clue came from black holes. In ordinary matter, the information a region can hold grows with its volume. In the 1970s, [Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole_thermodynamics) found that a black hole's entropy grows with its surface area instead. Entropy here measures how much information the black hole hides. The [holographic principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holographic_principle) turns that result into a proposal for any region of space. Everything inside could be described by information on its boundary, the way a flat hologram stores a three-dimensional image.

The strongest evidence is mathematical. In the late 1990s, three papers proposed that two model worlds describe the same physics. One is a universe with gravity inside [anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space), a curved space whose infinite expanse can be pictured inside a snow globe. The other is a quantum theory with no gravity, living on the surface of that globe. [Quanta Magazine](https://www.quantamagazine.org/gravity-seems-holographic-what-does-that-mean-for-reality-20260925/) calls this [correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AdS/CFT_correspondence) nearly a mathematical fact.
