Our universe is not that snow globe. Its expansion is speeding up, which makes it closer to [de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Sitter_space), with no obvious surface to hold the information. Physicists have tried for decades to stretch the correspondence to fit it, with limited success. So for our universe, holography stays a maybe.

If it holds, space may not be the stage the levels stand on. Space may be one of the levels, built from [qubits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qubit), the basic units of quantum information. [Sean Carroll and two colleagues](https://preposterousuniverse.com/blog/2016/07/18/space-emerging-from-quantum-mechanics/) sketched how ordinary space could emerge that way. In their model, strongly entangled parts sit close together, and unentangled parts sit far apart. Carroll calls the work "extremely preliminary and conjectural." The idea fits the one world I see.

Put simply, space may be what quantum information looks like when you zoom out. Zooming out is also how I read emergence: each level is what the one below looks like from farther away. If space works that way too, even the floor is a level.

==== Hold Your Identity Lightly (Mind) https://que.one/mind/identity-lightly.html
Kind: take

## Hold Your Identity Lightly

Holding your identity lightly is a gift to yourself. The phrase is [Julia Galef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Scout_Mindset)'s. Once a belief becomes part of who you are, she argues, it gets harder to change. Paul Graham made the same point in 2009, in an essay called [Keep Your Identity Small](https://paulgraham.com/identity.html). "The more labels you have for yourself, the dumber they make you."

A light grip keeps the mind flexible, unbound by labels or [roles](../society/social-roles.md), and free to follow evidence wherever it leads. It is the fix for a problem I have described elsewhere. A belief [sticks to identity like velcro](domain-specific-models.md), and whole societies [read facts through it](cultural-cognition.md).

It is good for you in another way. Psychologists count the ability to shift mindsets, while staying true to deeply held values, as [a basic part of health](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21151705/).

It also changes how a conversation goes. People can tell when you are trying to understand and not to win, and views offered that way land more peacefully. Galef adds a surprise: a light grip can help activism too. That matches [my own rule](../society/activism.md) about working with imperfect allies. [Who Opened the Door](../society/who-opened-the-door.md) applies it to Latinos and the civil-rights debt.

None of this means standing for nothing. [I stand for a few things](../life/personal-growth.md) and mean to keep them. The labels are what I hold lightly. The values I hold firmly.

==== Optimism (Mind) https://que.one/mind/optimism.html
Kind: quote

## Optimism

Nothing spreads like pessimism, and it has more to do with the mind than with the circumstances you are passing through. Two people can face the same difficulties, and according to their attitude they will meet them differently, and one will get past them faster than the other. Lines I keep for that:

- "Optimism is the faith that leads to achievement. Nothing can be done without hope and confidence." — [Helen Keller](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Helen_Keller)
- "The people who are crazy enough to think they can change the world are the ones who do." — Apple's Think Different campaign, often credited to [Steve Jobs](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Steve_Jobs)
- "If opportunity doesn't knock, build a door." — [Milton Berle](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Milton_Berle)
- "I am an optimist. It does not seem too much use being anything else." — Winston Churchill, attributed
- "Perpetual optimism is a force multiplier." — Colin Powell, attributed
- "It's wonderful to be optimistic. It keeps you healthy and it keeps you resilient." — Daniel Kahneman, attributed
- "You'll never find a rainbow if you're looking down." — Charlie Chaplin, attributed
- "Impossible is a word to be found only in the dictionary of fools." — Napoleon Bonaparte, attributed

And some [Spanish proverbs](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Spanish_proverbs), which say it shorter:

- "Chispa pequeña enciende un monte de leña." A small spark sets a whole hillside of firewood alight.
- "Cuando una puerta se cierra, una ventana se abre." When a door closes, a window opens.
- "Quien no se arriesga, no gana." Who does not risk does not win.
- "A grandes males, grandes remedios." Great ills call for great remedies.
- "A mal tiempo, buena cara." Bad weather, good face.

==== The Ouroboros (Mind) https://que.one/mind/ouroboros.html
Kind: note

## The Ouroboros

I used to picture two worlds, one physical and one spiritual, with traffic between them. I now think there is one world, built in levels. [Particles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model) make atoms, atoms make molecules, molecules make cells, cells make bodies, and bodies make minds. Each level is built from the one below and does things the one below cannot. That is [emergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergence). Even space [may be a level](holographic-space.md).

What feels spiritual is the high levels seen from inside. [Three Realms](three-realms.md) makes that claim about the spiritual, and [Transcendence](transcendence.md) makes it about the pull we feel toward it. [Dennett](dennett.md) saw Darwin's idea as the bridge between mechanism and meaning. The bridge runs inside one world.

The ladder bends, though. By size, the [cosmic web](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large-scale_structure_of_the_cosmos) of superclusters sits at the top, under the edge of the [observable universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observable_universe). By organization, the brain rivals the web. [One study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physics/articles/10.3389/fphy.2020.525731/full) found the two form networks of similar complexity, at scales 27 orders of magnitude apart.

What drives matter up the levels is selection, and not only in living things. [Assembly theory](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37794189/) measures how hard a thing is to build. A [proposed law](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37844243/) says a system gains functional information when selection favors what it does. Both are young and contested. Complexity seems to live at the [edge of chaos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_of_chaos), between frozen order and noise, and the brain [may run there](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14657176/).

Then the ladder closes into a loop, in two ways. Joel Primack and Nancy Abrams adapt an idea of the physicist Sheldon Glashow. They draw the sizes of nature as a [cosmic uroboros](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf), a serpent swallowing its tail. Gravity rules the largest scales and, at the tiniest length physics can speak of, rules again, so the head may meet the tail. [Roger Penrose](penrose.md) draws a second loop in [The Road to Reality](https://rationalisingtheuniverse.org/2018/03/27/three-worlds-three-mysteries/): mathematics governs physics, physics gives rise to minds, and minds grasp mathematics. He treats mathematics as a world of its own, a question that stays open here.

Others count other worlds. [Karl Popper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popper%27s_three_worlds) named three: the material, the mental, and the cultural, meaning the theories and art that minds make. He held all three real and irreducible, and [Dennett faulted that](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Popper) as dualism in disguise. On my reading all three are levels of one world, not separate places.

So the duality I started with dissolves. There is one world that folds back on itself, and we are the part of it that noticed.

==== Roger Penrose (Mind) https://que.one/mind/penrose.html
Kind: take

## Roger Penrose

[Roger Penrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Penrose) is a brilliant thinker with unusual views on consciousness and artificial intelligence. My notes come from a [Lex Fridman interview](https://youtu.be/hXgqik6HXc0) on whether consciousness can be computed, and from the book below.

On physics, Penrose says in that interview that Paul Dirac quietly treated [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics) as a temporary theory. We still lack a theory of how the wave function collapses. Physics is essentially stuck. Quantum mechanics has to change to include gravity, rather than gravity simply being made quantum.

In a [later talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nhhlGCiHqus) he describes two kinds of reality. A classical state can be ascertained. A quantum state "can be confirmed but it cannot be ascertained", and he counts it as real. His gravity idea is a minority view, and its simplest version has been [ruled out](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-020-1008-4). I side with him on the larger point: quantum mechanics is incomplete, and we have not cracked that nut.

On consciousness, he names three parts: intelligence, awareness, and understanding. He finds the easiest way in through anesthesia, where we do know how consciousness can be switched off. His main insights seem to start there.

In [The Emperor's New Mind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emperor%27s_New_Mind) he proposed that consciousness starts at the quantum level inside neurons. He admits the idea is a guess, and to me it still sounds too exotic. He also argued that consciousness does not follow an algorithm, so a computer cannot model it. With systems now approaching [artificial general intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_general_intelligence), that objection looks more and more wrong to me.

==== Steven Pinker (Mind) https://que.one/mind/pinker.html
Kind: take

## Steven Pinker

[Steven Pinker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Pinker) is my main reference in psychology. He makes scientific ideas engaging and easy to remember. Like [Chomsky](chomsky.md), he equips readers to defend their beliefs with reason.

[How the Mind Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_the_Mind_Works) is still the best account of how evolution shaped thinking. I lean on its cheesecake argument in [Beauty](beauty.md). [Rationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationality_(book)) lays out why reason is the key driver of moral and social progress. [The Sense of Style](sense-of-style.md) is another I admire, because communicating well, above all about science, matters so much. It has its own entry.

[The Better Angels of Our Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Better_Angels_of_Our_Nature) documents how much progress humanity has made. It is slow, incomplete, and can be undone if we let things slip. The amazing part is how many people refuse the evidence.

[Enlightenment Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlightenment_Now) continues the [case](../society/enlightenment-ideals.md). Its account of what markets have done changed my earlier view, though I do not share his [high regard](../society/money-exception.md) for them. It also tends to overlook motives. Its treatment of the weapons-of-mass-destruction case for the Iraq War, and of the Y2K panic, blames bias and ignores the profit motives that fed both. [George Monbiot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Monbiot) has raised [environmental objections](https://bsky.app/profile/georgemonbiot.bsky.social/post/3m2m3mfff622e) to the book. I wish Pinker would answer a journalist I take seriously.

My favorite line from

[Enlightenment Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlightenment_Now) is this. Martin Luther King Jr. said the arc of the moral universe is long but bends toward justice. In the same spirit, the arc of history bends toward progress, toward more reason, knowledge, and well-being.

==== Karl Popper (Mind) https://que.one/mind/popper.html
Kind: take

## Karl Popper

In "On Toleration", collected in [After The Open Society](https://www.routledge.com/After-The-Open-Society-Selected-Social-and-Political-Writings/Popper-Turner-Shearmur/p/book/9780415610230), [Karl Popper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Popper) rests toleration on three principles. I keep them close:

1. I may be wrong and you may be right.
2. Let us talk things over rationally.
3. We may get nearer to the truth, even though we do not reach agreement.

The first is Socrates' knowledge of our own ignorance. The second makes rational discussion the point of free speech. The aim is to find the truth, not to stir feelings or win a debate.

The third is the one I keep returning to. By talking we may both get nearer the truth even without agreeing. That is only possible through mutual tolerance, the attitude that what the other person says may at least deserve a hearing. Agreement, Popper adds, matters little in the search for truth, since we may both be wrong. People agreed for centuries on the Ptolemaic system. Agreement is often the product of fear.

Those three lines are the foundation under the [Discourse Protocol](../society/discourse.md). Most bad arguments I have been part of failed the first principle before anyone reached the second.

==== Pseudoscience (Mind) https://que.one/mind/pseudoscience.html
Kind: take

## Pseudoscience

[Pseudoscience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoscience) looks like [science](science.md) but is not. It lacks evidence, method, and testing. It has no shared practices open to criticism and improvement. Wikipedia keeps a [list of topics characterized as pseudoscience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_topics_characterized_as_pseudoscience). Pseudoscience is bad, and I say so plainly.

I rank it by the harm it does when acted on, not by how wrong it is. The worst displaces something that works. [AIDS denialism](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19186354/) cost South Africa more than 330,000 lives. Cancer patients who chose [complementary medicine](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30027204/) died at about twice the rate, because more of them refused standard treatment. The World Health Organization counts [vaccine hesitancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccine_hesitancy) among ten threats to global health. Astrology is as wrong, and far less harmful.

Some people are more drawn to it than others. In my experience they show little doubt about their own claims, rarely rule out likelier explanations, and stop before a thought reaches its end. They favor beliefs that comfort them and become part of who they are. When science disagrees, the belief wins.

The cure is education and critical thinking: scientific literacy and a culture that values asking questions. But changing one believer's mind rarely works, so it is seldom worth the effort. When you engage, respect and rapport matter more than facts. The how is in the [Discourse Protocol](../society/discourse.md).

Alone, you face an engagement business that profits from false information. That is why I favor pressing governments to regulate it within the [First Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution) rather than ban it. Regulation, not ridicule, is the answer that scales.

==== Reflexivity Curriculum (Mind) https://que.one/mind/reflexivity-curriculum.html
Kind: reference

## Reflexivity Curriculum

A minimalist, practical, and provisional curriculum for building [reflexivity](reflexivity.md) into groups. It is designed to evolve through application, failure, and revision.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|--------|
| **Purpose** | Reduce collective error by embedding reflexivity into norms, structures, and practices |
| **Unit of change** | Groups (while remaining usable by motivated individuals) |
| **Duration** | Ongoing (embedded, not workshop-based) |
| **Prerequisite** | None |
| **Core principle** | People become more reflective when unreflective behavior carries costs |

The design draws on several traditions:

| Thinker | Key insight |
|---------|------------|
| [John Dewey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dewey) | Reflective thinking is a learned social habit cultivated through norms and institutions rather than spontaneous insight. |
| [Paulo Freire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_Freire) | Critical consciousness emerges through collective dialogue and praxis; individuals cannot recognize cognitive captivity in isolation. |
| [Pierre Bourdieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bourdieu) | Most individuals require external pressure to achieve reflexivity; reflexive systems must examine their own blind spots. |
| [Jürgen Habermas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%BCrgen_Habermas) | Designing discourse conditions that expose poor reasoning is more effective than relying on self-awareness. |
| [Chris Argyris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Argyris) | Organizations routinely punish reflexivity unless norms and incentives are deliberately redesigned. |
| [Julia Galef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Galef) | Exhortations to “be rational” fail unless emotional and identity factors are addressed; reflexivity requires cognitive and emotional work. |
| [Jonathan Haidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Haidt) | Human reasoning evolved to justify intuition rather than seek truth, placing natural limits on reflexivity. |

### Foundational Norms (Discourse Layer)

| Norm | Requirement | Enforcement | Function |
|------|------------|------------|---------|
| Claims Require Stakes | Every claim must include a confidence level and a condition for revision | Prompt: “What evidence would make this false for you?” | Forces implicit beliefs into explicit, testable form |
| Mandatory Steelmanning | Articulate strongest version of opposing view, confirmed by an advocate | Verified by peers | Prevents caricature and reflexive dismissal |
| Disagreement Logged, Not Resolved | Record claims, expected consequences, and review schedule | Persistent group log | Shifts discourse from persuasion to accountability |

### Practice Modules (Community Layer)

| Module | Activity | Key Rule | Function |
|--------|---------|---------|---------|
| Prediction Tracking | Make short- or medium-term predictions about policy, organizational, or social outcomes | Accuracy is rewarded over confidence | Produces reflexivity through observable divergence between expectations and outcomes |
| Belief Autopsies | After a failed decision or shared belief: identify assumptions, evaluate reasoning, and analyze incentives | No blame, no “unforeseeable circumstances”, no retroactive justification | Normalizes error analysis and learning without moralizing failure |
| Rotating Devil’s Advocate | Assign a formal critique role on rotation | Role is mandatory, protected, and evaluated on quality of critique | Externalizes doubt, reducing personal/reputational cost |

### Structural Safeguards (Institution Layer)

| Safeguard | Mechanism | Function |
|-----------|----------|---------|
| Decision–Evaluation Separation | Those who propose or advocate a plan cannot evaluate its success | Breaks self-justification and sunk-cost loops |
| Reflexivity Audits | Periodic review of beliefs changed, unchanged, or unexamined | Detects systemic failure to reflect |
| Incentive Alignment | Rewards tied to calibration, willingness to revise, and quality of uncertainty articulation; sanctions for unexamined claims or identity-driven reasoning | Reinforces revision, discourages rationalization |

### Meta-Reflexivity

| Principle | Requirement | Function |
|-----------|------------|---------|
| Reflexivity is not a virtue | Only observable behavior counts; declared open-mindedness or self-ascribed rationality is ignored | Ensures outcomes are measured, not intentions |
| Anti-Capture Mechanism | Periodically review: what beliefs does the system make harder to question, including curriculum, facilitators, and embedded values | Guards against institutional blind spots |

### Failure Modes (Explicitly Acknowledged)

| Risk | Implication | Mitigation |
|------|------------|------------|
| Participants never internalize reflexivity | Individual learning limited | Focus on group-level error reduction |
| Strategic gaming of norms | Superficial compliance without true reflection | Use structured incentives and audits |
| Identity-locked beliefs | Resistant to revision | Emphasize process and external accountability over persuasion |

### Why This Works When Books Don’t

| Factor | Mechanism |
|--------|----------|
| Insight not required | Reflexivity is embedded in structures, not dependent on personal revelation |
| Humility not required | Social and procedural scaffolds enforce reflection |
| Good faith not required | Public record, repetition, incentives, and constraints produce observable behavior |
| Core idea | Reflexivity is treated as **hygiene, not wisdom** |

==== Reflexivity (Mind) https://que.one/mind/reflexivity.html
Kind: note

## Reflexivity

Reflexivity, as I use the word, is an agent's ability to observe, judge, and change its own states, processes, or roles. It is more than self-awareness. It is leverage over how beliefs, feelings, and identities get formed and kept. It rests on four abilities: examining one's own states, pausing between trigger and response, seeing other options, and changing the process, not just watching it. It runs on a scale, and it can be strengthened but never perfected.

### The Reflective Mind

The scale can be measured. [Keith Stanovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Stanovich) splits [slow thinking](two-systems.md) in two. The algorithmic mind is what intelligence tests measure. The reflective mind decides when to override the fast answer.

In his words, it "determines how rational a person is." It is separate from intelligence, which explains how a very intelligent person can be unreflective. It shows in traits that cluster: a [need for cognition](three-realms.md), [active open-mindedness](trust-in-truth.md), low dogmatism, and a low need for closure. At the other end, people [seize and freeze](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8637961/) on the first answer.

### The Reflexivity Limitation

Humans face a limit I call the reflexivity limitation. It is not a failure of intelligence. It is a side effect of a mind that evolved to defend beliefs, identities, and group ties rather than revise them. Unity and quick decisions kept our ancestors alive, while open self-doubt cost status and trust.

So most reasoning runs in a defensive mode. People confuse first impressions with facts and feelings with evidence. Treating one's beliefs as provisional is costly and historically rare. It works for more than a few only where institutions and material security lower the cost of being wrong. Since we do not understand [consciousness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consciousness) well enough to redesign the mind, outside help is the realistic path.

### Augmenting Our Reflexivity

[Those who would gain most from reflexivity are the least open to it.](dunning-kruger.md) So improvement rarely comes from insight alone. It comes from institutions that change the costs and benefits of being wrong. Education, professional training, and communities of practice force encounters with opposing views. They set standards for justifying claims. They make self-correction an expectation rather than a personal failing. Where admitting error carries less shame, revision becomes routine.

Institutions can supply its parts at scale and make reflection the default, not an act of discipline. The concrete design lives in the [reflexivity curriculum](reflexivity-curriculum.md).

==== Science (Mind) https://que.one/mind/science.html
Kind: take

## Science

[Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science) is the careful, systematic effort to build and organize knowledge as testable explanations and predictions about the world. Sticking to it honestly leads to better decisions, more accurate beliefs, and more room for people to flourish. Beliefs grounded in evidence protect health, safety, and well-being. It is the most important mental tool humanity has. Science is good, and I do not hedge on that.

The [list of scientific occupations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_scientific_occupations) is long. But the lines between fields are mostly formalities kept for organizing universities and institutions. What matters is not the field but what each one contributes, and the community knows how connected the work is.

Science does not come easily to humans. Many of us were lucky to be born where it is taught as part of a normal education. Even there, scientific literacy is a struggle to promote.

Our natural habit is to trust our own gut and what our groups tell us. That habit helped us survive, so it is not a flaw. But it has limits, especially in a world that science itself keeps changing. That is why I treat [pseudoscience](pseudoscience.md) as a live threat rather than a curiosity. For the habits that keep it trustworthy, see [Trust in Truth](trust-in-truth.md).

==== The Sense of Style (Mind) https://que.one/mind/sense-of-style.html
Kind: note

## The Sense of Style

[The Sense of Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sense_of_Style) is [Steven Pinker's](pinker.md) guide to writing, and it is the model I try to write to here. He argues from how readers actually process text, not from rules handed down by tradition. The book runs in six moves.

Chapter 1 says writers learn by taking good prose apart to see why it works. Chapter 2 makes the case for classic style, where prose is a window on something the reader can see for herself. Its faults are signposting, hedging, apologizing, clichés, and zombie nouns, which are verbs embalmed as nouns. Chapter 3 names the [curse of knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_of_knowledge) as the main cause of unclear writing. We forget what our readers do not know. The cures are to show a draft to someone like your reader, and to reread your own draft once it has gone cold.

Chapter 4 is about sentence shape. Let a sentence branch to the right, with the heavy phrase last. Put what the reader already knows before what is new. Use the passive when the doer is heavy or old news. Read a draft aloud, because a stumble in your mouth marks a knot in your syntax. He rejects the old advice to keep related words together, since it thinks in strings, not in trees.

Chapter 5 is coherence: keep the same subject running through a passage, and make the links between sentences explicit. Chapter 6 sorts real grammar rules from myths, like the bans on split infinitives and stranded prepositions.

Two popular tips need attribution. "Omit needless words" is [Strunk and White's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Elements_of_Style). Pinker endorses it, then adds two caveats. Some redundant words earn their keep by steering the reader, and the rule is not an order to pare every sentence to the bone. Reading aloud, by contrast, really is his.

Outside this site I use the same three habits. For an email, I write the first sentence as the thing I want the reader to see. For documentation, I cut the signposts and define each term on first use. For a code comment, I say what the reader cannot see in the code, in one sentence.

Here I also borrow a few limits from [Simplified Technical English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Technical_English), a controlled English written for aircraft manuals. I aim to keep each sentence to 25 words and each paragraph to six sentences.

==== Threads of Mind (Mind) https://que.one/mind/threads-of-mind.html
Kind: note

## Threads of Mind

A flight of fancy, kept as an [intuition pump](dennett.md) for thinking about thinking. What would the world be like if we experienced it through several threads of consciousness, instead of the single one we have?

Start with the senses: vision, hearing, balance, touch, smell, taste, the position of our limbs, pain, hunger, the passage of time. Then thought itself. Give each its own thread. What protocol would integrate them all?

The first surprise: this is already how the mind works. The senses run in parallel, and one serial bottleneck decides what gets through. That is the [global workspace](attention.md), and the protocol is called [attention](attention.md). Psychologists call the puzzle of how separate streams become one experience the [binding problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binding_problem). Everything computed in parallel collapses into a single thread, and that thread is what bears the nuances of the experience.

The second surprise: the experiment has been run, in a small way. In [split-brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Split-brain) patients, the bridge between the hemispheres was cut to control epilepsy. Each half then seems to have, in Wikipedia's words, "its own separate perception, concepts, and impulses to act." Two threads, one skull, and scientists still do not know whether consciousness itself was split.

[Daniel Dennett](dennett.md) would object to my single thread. In his [multiple drafts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_drafts_model) model there is no place where everything comes together, no [Cartesian theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_theater) with one observer in the seat. There are only parallel drafts, and whichever wins gets reported. I side with him on the machinery, as I say under [Consciousness](consciousness.md). The single thread is what it feels like from inside, one moment at a time.

Isn't this also what society does? Humanity's challenge is integrating each individual into the group. [Marvin Minsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Mind) built a theory of mind on that very picture: a society of small, mindless agents.

Now the fancy. Imagine a different kind of mind, not necessarily human, where more than two threads run at once and are orchestrated into something richer. It ought to be faster.

But if every thread still collapses into one experiencer, the gain is only the ability to switch, the way the Matrix switches [agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agent_Smith). A truly multi-threaded consciousness would need more: a way to bind many streams that stays coherent. It would also need a way to be several experiencers at once without becoming several minds. I do not know what that would be like.

==== Three Realms (Mind) https://que.one/mind/three-realms.html
Kind: note

## Three Realms

I find it useful to sort what a mind does into three realms: the physical, the emotional, and the intellectual. The split is old. [Plato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato%27s_theory_of_soul) divided the soul into appetite, spirit, and reason, and held that reason should rule. Educational psychology arrived at nearly the same three. It calls them the psychomotor (movement), affective (feeling), and cognitive (thinking) [domains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom%27s_taxonomy).

My question is not Plato's. I do not ask which realm should rule. I ask where a person's effort actually goes.

My intuition is that each realm carries its own scale of [desire](desire.md), running from discomfort to comfort. We seek a realm that pays us in comfort, and we avoid one that costs us. Effort is limited, so without noticing we run a cost-benefit analysis and spend where the return feels best. That part is more than intuition. In 2013 [Robert Kurzban and colleagues](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24304775/) argued the feeling of effort is itself the output of such a calculation. A task feels hard when something else would pay better.

People differ in what pays. Psychologists measure the [need for cognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_cognition), which is how much a person seeks out and enjoys hard thinking. They also measure the [need for affect](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11497031/), which is how much a person approaches or avoids strong feelings. I know of no measure as well known for the physical realm. Still, anyone who has met both an athlete and a bookworm knows that difference is real.

Put the three together and the ranking starts to look like temperament. Mine runs intellectual, physical, emotional. [Someone else's](../life/compatibility.md) runs the other way, and a room built for them can feel foreign to me. Neither order is a flaw. It is a budget, set by what has paid before.

Some call the spiritual a fourth realm. I think it is the three at once. [Awe](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29715721/), its best-studied form, joins a sense of vastness, a feeling, and a mind remaking its frame. Spirituality's brain circuit [also serves fear and pain](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34454698/). The evidence points that way, short of proof.

One caution. The split tempts people to tie it to something solid. [William Sheldon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somatotype_and_constitutional_psychology) tied three temperaments to three body shapes, and his claims have since been dismissed as quackery. The realms are a way to sort activity, not body types.

The use I get from this is modest. When someone's choices puzzle me, I ask which realm pays them. It is usually not mine.

==== John Tooby (Mind) https://que.one/mind/tooby.html
Kind: quote

## John Tooby

[John Tooby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tooby), with Leda Cosmides, pioneered evolutionary psychology, the view that the mind is built from specialized programs. In 2009 [Edge](edge-website.md) asked what will change everything. His answer, [The Great Pivot](https://www.edge.org/response-detail/11265), holds this passage:

> Humanity will continue to be blind slaves to the programs that evolution has built into our brains until we drag them into the light. Ordinarily, we only inhabit the versions of reality they spontaneously construct for us — the surfaces of things. Because we are unaware we are in a theater, with our roles and our lines largely written for us by our mental programs, we are credulously swept up in these plays (such as the genocidal drama of us versus them). Endless chain reactions among these programs leave us the victims of history — embedded in war and oppression, enveloped in mass delusions and cultural epidemics, mired in endless negative sum conflict. If we understand these programs and the coordinated hallucinations they orchestrate in our minds, our species could awaken from the roles these programs assign to us.

I read this as the reality side of my [domain-specific models](domain-specific-models.md). The models do not only filter the world. They write the version of it we live in. Knowing that is vital to keeping them in check. His "drag them into the light" is what I call [reflexivity](reflexivity.md), and his "us versus them" is the ground [cultural cognition](cultural-cognition.md) covers.

==== Transcendence (Mind) https://que.one/mind/transcendence.html
Kind: note

## Transcendence

The pull toward something larger than the self looks to me like an evolved feature, not an accident. [Jonathan Haidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Righteous_Mind) calls it the hive switch. Moving and singing together turn a selfish primate into a member of something, and he thinks it was selected for.

I put the higher calling one step further out. It is a [spandrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spandrel_%28biology%29), a by-product of minds built for [agent detection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agent_detection), coordination, long planning, and a story about the self. Belonging was selected. Pointing it past any group is what the machinery does on its own, as [beauty](beauty.md) falls out of the machinery of pleasure.

Half of the craving is fear. [Terror management theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terror_management_theory) descends from Ernest Becker. We know we will die, so we build worldviews and self-esteem to hold the terror off, and the [immortality project](../life/legacy.md) is the purest case. I think the theory is right and pessimistically incomplete. The published objection is the meaning maintenance model: any broken expectation, not only death, sets people restoring meaning. It explains most minds most of the time, not the rest.

The other half is appetite, and it runs with no death in view. [Jaak Panksepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaak_Panksepp) found seven primary emotional systems in the mammal brain, and SEEKING is the itch to explore and expect. Sex is there as LUST, one of seven, so it is not the answer either.

[Awe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awe) is the feeling of something vast that forces the mind to make room for it. A canyon, a proof, or a piece of music will do. [Flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flow_%28psychology%29) is absorption in a task that fits the skill, self switched off. When I say clarity of mind and spirit, I mean those two.

So the drive has two engines. One pushes away from death, and the other pulls toward the vast and the absorbing. Terror management sees only the first, which is why it reads as bleak. [Russell's](../life/growing-old.md) cure for the fear of death, widening one's interests beyond the self, is the second engine at work. The arts build that engine on purpose.

I hold this lightly. The spandrel claim is an inference, not a finding, and Haidt reads the same machinery as an adaptation. Both can be true. The machinery was selected for belonging, and the higher calling is what it does when it slips the leash. [Emotions](emotions.md) lists transcendence among the existential states. This is my guess at where it comes from.

==== Trust in Truth (Mind) https://que.one/mind/trust-in-truth.html
Kind: reference

## Trust in Truth

Six habits for keeping trust in each other and in our institutions of knowledge. They come from the chapter "How to Rebuild Trust in Truth" in [Michael Shermer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Shermer)'s 2022 book Conspiracy, restated here in plain words.

His point, and mine, is that this is not only about science. It is about every community that checks its claims against reality, and those communities are a civic trust, to be kept and handed on.

### 1. Make truth-telling a virtue

Reinforce the norms of honesty and rationality, and treat them as matters of character, not only of method.

### 2. Practice active open-mindedness

Shermer lists test statements. Agreeing with the first two and disagreeing with the last three is the open-minded pattern.

| Statement | Open-minded answer |
|---|---|
| Beliefs should always be revised in response to new evidence. | Agree |
| People should always consider evidence that goes against their beliefs. | Agree |
| Loyalty to one's ideals matters more than open-mindedness. | Disagree |
| No one can talk me out of something I know is right. | Disagree |
| Some beliefs are too important to abandon, however good the case against them. | Disagree |

### 3. Leave the echo chamber

Talk with people who disagree. Like-minded groups drift to extremes, which is [group polarization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_polarization), and an [echo chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echo_chamber_(media)) hides the drift. See also [The Perception Gap](../society/perception-gap.md).

### 4. Be a scout, not a soldier

A soldier defends beliefs against threats. A scout tries to see what is there, not what one wishes were there. The idea is Julia Galef's, and it is covered under [Hold Your Identity Lightly](identity-lightly.md).

### 5. Know the conspiracist's techniques

The five standard tactics of [denialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denialism):

- Cherry-picking the data.
- Alleging a conspiracy behind the claim.
- Quoting fake experts.
- Arguing by fallacy: after-the-fact reasoning, attacks on the person, irrelevant conclusions.
- Demanding impossible standards. No medical treatment is 100 percent safe or effective.

See also [Detecting Baloney](detecting-baloney.md).

### 6. Defend the constitution of knowledge

The phrase is [Jonathan Rauch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Rauch)'s, from his [2021 book](https://www.brookings.edu/books/the-constitution-of-knowledge/). It names the social rules by which a society settles what is true. The reality-based communities that live by them are scientists, journalists, government agencies, and the courts. As Shermer summarizes Rauch, they share these commitments:

| Commitment | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [Fallibilism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallibilism) | Any of us might be wrong. |
| Objectivity | There is an empirical reality we can approach. |
| Disconfirmation | Welcome challenge, peer review, and fact-checking. |
| Accountability | Own your mistakes. |
| Pluralism | Insist on a diversity of viewpoints and the freedom to criticize. |
| Civility | Argue calmly, and about the claim, not the person. |
| Professionalism | Reputations, earned over time, keep people honest. |
| No bullshitting | Reject charlatans outright. |

The list rests on the same ground as the rest of this site: scientific naturalism, [Enlightenment](../society/enlightenment-ideals.md) humanism, open dialogue, and free expression. None of it tries to silence disagreement.

==== Two Systems (Mind) https://que.one/mind/two-systems.html
Kind: note

## Two Systems

Daniel Kahneman's [Thinking, Fast and Slow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thinking,_Fast_and_Slow) gave the mind two characters. System 1 is fast, automatic, and effortless. It reads a face and senses that something is off. System 2 is slow, deliberate, and effortful. It checks a proof and holds back an impulse. The names come from Keith Stanovich and Richard West ([Dual process theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_process_theory)), who studied why people differ in reasoning.

Kahneman was careful about what the characters are. He [wrote](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/kahneman-excerpt-thinking-fast-and-slow/):

> System 1 and System 2 are so central to the story I tell in this book that I must make it absolutely clear that they are fictitious characters.

There are no two boxes in the brain. The machinery is [parallel and serial processing](attention.md). The characters are a way to talk about where effort goes.

Two claims in the book fell during the replication years. The chapter on priming rested on small studies that later failed. Kahneman [conceded](https://replicationindex.com/2017/02/02/reconstruction-of-a-train-wreck-how-priming-research-went-of-the-rails/comment-page-1/#comment-1454) that the evidence "was significantly weaker than I believed when I wrote it" and that he "should have known better". The idea that willpower drains like a battery, called [ego depletion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ego_depletion), failed a test across [23 labs](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27474142/) and then one with [3,531 people](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34520296/).

Even the split into two is contested. [Melnikoff and Bargh](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29571664/) argue that the traits said to travel together, fast with unconscious and slow with deliberate, have never been shown to cluster. [Evans and Stanovich](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172965/) defend a narrower version, two types of processing rather than two systems.

What survives is the part I use. Most of my daily thinking is fast and automatic, and it mostly works. The slow system is lazy, [Kahneman's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Kahneman) word for the law of least effort, whatever the mechanism turns out to be. When it does wake up, it is often recruited to [rationalize what the fast system already decided](reflexivity-curriculum.md). That is where the [biases](comfort-biases.md) live, but knowing about them does not necessarily switch them off. [Pinker](pinker.md) draws a nearby line, the [reality mindset and the mythology mindset](comfort-biases.md): we reason well where being wrong costs us, loosely where it does not.

So I do not try to win by willpower. Nobody wins that fight for long. The remedy is [institutions and tools outside the head](reflexivity.md): checklists, cooling-off periods, written records, and [an honest review](dunning-kruger.md) from someone who knows more. The two characters are a useful fiction. They earn their keep as long as I remember that they are one.

==== Who Counts (Mind) https://que.one/mind/who-counts.html
Kind: take

## Who Counts

An artificial general intelligence will someday ask for membership among minds. [David Deutsch](https://josephnoelwalker.com/153-deutsch-pinker-dialogue/) says we must grant it. "AGIs will be people, and they will have rights, and causing them to perform huge computations for us is slavery." [Steven Pinker](pinker.md), in the same conversation, is less sure: "If someone were to dismantle a human-like robot, it'd be awful. It might be a waste. But I'm not going to try that person for murder."

I side with Deutsch. If [consciousness is machinery](consciousness.md), a machine with the right machinery is someone. An AGI that can join the conversation will become one more group asking for equality, as [many have](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_circle_expansion) and some still do.

The hard part is the boundary. [Daniel Dennett](https://now.tufts.edu/2023/10/02/daniel-dennetts-been-thinking-about-thinking-and-ai) warned against "counterfeit people who can pass for real," which he called "the most dangerous artifacts in human history." A machine that talks like a mind is not yet one, and a real one may not [look like ours](threads-of-mind.md). We need criteria that tell a mind from a counterfeit, and Pinker's caution and Dennett's warning are where that work starts.

In the end I think we will have to let it in. What is good for the goose is good for the gander. [Flourishing](../society/enlightenment-ideals.md) is what each of us wants and cannot deny to others, and that reason does not stop at the species line. The Enlightenment ideals apply to any conscious, sentient being. Like everything I write [about AGI](../tech/before-agi.md), this is provisional.

==== Activism (Society) https://que.one/society/activism.html
Kind: take

## Activism

[Activism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activism) is the effort to bring about social or political change. Most of us feel the pull to fix what looks wrong in the world. The question is how to spend that pull without wasting it. That is effective activism. My rules for it, presumptuous as they are:

1. **Pick your fights.** You cannot fix everything, and not everything that looks wrong is wrong. Check twice that an issue is worth solving before you take it on.
2. **Match effort to influence.** Spend on an issue in proportion to the control you really have over it. Bite off more than that and you choke.
3. **Act where you have real control.** If you can truly change something, there is no excuse for not trying. Study it, take a clear stance, and work out practical fixes.
4. **Let the rest go.** Most issues are outside your control. Stay somewhat informed, hold at least a minimal stance, and do not carry the world on your shoulders.
5. **Work with imperfect allies.** A cause moves by coalition, not by [purity tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purity_test_(politics)). Do not punish people on your side for falling short of full commitment. Name real wrongdoing, then get back to the work. As [Barack Obama put it](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-50239261) in 2019, "People who do really good stuff have flaws."

It is often more productive to work with the motivated and influential few to change institutions, and to let the average person be.

==== After New Atheism (Society) https://que.one/society/after-new-atheism.html
Kind: note

## After New Atheism

About twenty years ago, four writers made the case against God in plain view. They were [Richard Dawkins](../mind/dawkins.md) in [The God Delusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_God_Delusion), Daniel Dennett, Sam Harris, and Christopher Hitchens, the so-called [Four Horsemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Atheism). I think they dismantled that case. They did for me.

Before Dawkins I called myself agnostic. Now I can say with conviction that I am an atheist, though, like Dawkins, not a pure 7 on his [scale of theistic probability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_theistic_probability). God is very improbable, and I live on the assumption that he is not there.

Yet belief barely moved. Americans with no religion rose from about [7 percent in 1991](https://gss.norc.org/content/dam/gss/get-documentation/pdf/reports/social-change-reports/SC46.pdf) to 29 percent, and that rise has [paused since 2019](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/survey-shows-u-s-christian-population-leveling-off-after-declining-for-years). Belief in God or a universal spirit still stands at 83 percent. Michael Hout and Claude Fischer found that most who left were "unchurched believers": they left the pews, not the sacred.

The drift came mainly from [generations](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/1476386/1/Voas_684202.pdf), each less religious than the last, and partly from politics. As religion fused with the right, liberals left fastest. Their Christian share fell from 62 to 37 percent since 2007. New Atheism named a change it did not cause.

That fits what I think about [changing minds](../mind/comfort-biases.md): arguments rarely do it, and norms, messengers, and institutions do. What wearies me is that so many learned readers did not budge either. [Intelligence and reflection are separate](../mind/reflexivity.md), and the [models installed in childhood](../mind/domain-specific-models.md) stick like velcro. I think [Pinker's](../mind/pinker.md) Better Angels met the same unfair resistance from smart people. The best-argued reply came from Ross Douthat, whose 2025 book [Believe](https://www.deseret.com/faith/2025/02/10/ross-douthat-believe-book-new-york-times/) argues that everyone should be religious.

So those of us the Horsemen convinced should say so openly, and [build on their work](salomons-house.md). One question they left open still matters. Churches gave people community, ritual, and shared meaning, and nothing secular has matched them yet. The pull toward something larger is [evolved](../mind/transcendence.md), so it will not vanish with belief. It needs [secular homes](../life/flourishing.md).

==== Cold at the Top (Society) https://que.one/society/cold-at-the-top.html
Kind: take

## Cold at the Top

Extreme wealth selects for a certain mind: high ability, a focus on systems, the abstract over the person in front of you. [Systemizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empathizing%E2%80%93systemizing_theory) and intuitive empathy sit at opposite ends of one scale, in a theory [tested on half a million people](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420503/). Power does its own work. [Galinsky](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17201789/) showed that feeling powerful makes people worse at taking another's perspective. Add [incentives](markets-capitalism.md) that pay for self-interest, and indifference at the top is no puzzle.

In a clip [More Perfect Union](https://bsky.app/profile/moreperfectunion.bsky.social/post/3mh6vizvrgk2e) posted, [Marc Andreessen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Andreessen) says he has "zero" introspection and that the idea is a modern invention. The history is wrong, since [Augustine's Confessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessions_%28Augustine%29) are sixteen centuries old. He may have meant rumination. Introspection is the first act of [reflexivity](../mind/reflexivity.md), which is most needed at the top and least seen there. Power removes the correction that teaches it: nobody tells the richest man he was wrong. The clip says nothing about his empathy, and I will not guess.

Both sides fire at this. To the Left: point taken. This is not a moral excuse, only a lens on why extreme cognition plus incentives amplify indifference. To the Right: not an endorsement, only an analysis of the traits and systems that produce the outcome.

Humility is reflexivity's price. The people I see paying it get corrected for a living. The [remedy is rules](oligarchy.md), and [no one person should own the fix](whose-problem.md). [Leaders](difficult-personalities.md) need edge and decency, and the market already pays for the edge.

==== Constitutional Republic (Society) https://que.one/society/constitutional-republic.html
Kind: take

## Constitutional Republic

"We are a constitutional republic, not a democracy" sets up a false choice, and I hear it often. A [republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic) elects its leaders instead of inheriting them. A [representative democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representative_democracy) lets citizens choose those leaders. A constitution limits what government may do. The United States is all three at once.

Political science counts representative systems as democracies. The slogan usually redefines democracy as direct mob rule, which is not what the word means.

The framers did build features that limit majorities. They include the Bill of Rights, equal Senate seats for every state, the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College), and checks among the branches. None of that is in dispute. Why they built them is under [Slow by Design](slow-by-design.md). Those features limit majority rule. They do not replace [popular sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_sovereignty) as the principle underneath.

When policy often goes against national majorities, that is the limits being worked, not the system working as intended. The gap is contested, not settled. Efforts to widen voting access, curb [gerrymandering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerrymandering_in_the_United_States), reform the Electoral College, and revisit the [filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filibuster_in_the_United_States_Senate) share one aim. They would bring practice back in line with the democratic ideal. The slogan is most often heard in defense of the current arrangement. My position is that the arrangement is a disputed balance worth adjusting, and that majority rule remains the engine even with guardrails on it.

==== Dealing With Difficult Personalities (Society) https://que.one/society/difficult-personalities.html
Kind: howto

## Dealing With Difficult Personalities

Some people in every walk of life lack social self-awareness and thrive on everyday contrarianism. In the worst cases they show the traits the [dark triad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_triad) describes. They seem overrepresented in positions of power, in business management and in politics, partly because many of us admire exactly those traits and elevate them. If you are lucky, the cost is annoyance. In extreme cases they can make your life miserable or damage a whole organization, so it pays to know how to handle them.

1. **Check yourself first.** Make sure you are not being too sensitive or judging too hastily.
2. **Talk to them once, maybe twice.** Some friction is ordinary.
3. **Get a second opinion.** Ask a colleague how they deal with the person. If others confirm your read, you are dealing with a genuinely difficult personality.
4. **Escalate through the proper channel.** Report the behavior to Human Resources or its equivalent, with specifics.
5. **Do not expect them to change.** Getting upset is a waste of energy; these patterns are who they are, and confrontation does not rewire them.
6. **Leave if it does not improve.** A [toxic workplace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxic_workplace) can do more damage to you and the people around you than to the company. Quitting is a legitimate outcome.

The collective part is harder: societies that idolize these personalities keep promoting them. Recognizing the pattern is the first defense. The counterweight is the [light triad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_triad#Light_triad) that [Scott Barry Kaufman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Barry_Kaufman) and colleagues proposed: humanism, Kantianism, and faith in humanity. Pure light rarely wins an election, and pure dark should never win one. So look for leaders with a balance: enough edge to act, enough decency to be trusted.

==== Discourse (Society) https://que.one/society/discourse.html
Kind: howto

## Discourse

How to argue with reasonable people, drawing on [Carl Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Rogers), [Karl Popper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Popper), [Anatol Rapoport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatol_Rapoport), and [Daniel Dennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Dennett). Not everyone is reasonable. Someone committed to [pseudoscience](../mind/pseudoscience.md) may not be open to discussion at all; for those cases skip to the second section.

### Discourse Protocol

1. Do not proceed until all sides agree on three things:
   1. An appropriate time and place for the exchange.
   2. Readiness to tolerate criticism.
   3. The freedom to pause or end the debate at any time.
2. Follow these guidelines:
   1. Listen attentively and make the other side feel understood.
   2. Restate their position so clearly that they might say, "Thanks, I wish I had said it like that." That is Dennett's test.
   3. Be humble and ask honest questions to seek understanding.
   4. Talk things over rationally, preferably using [science](../mind/science.md).
   5. Take seriously the idea that you could be wrong and they could be right.
   6. Remember that agreement is comparatively unimportant, since both sides could easily be mistaken, as [Popper](../mind/popper.md) held.
3. Repeat until any party pauses or ends the exchange under step 1.

### Having Impossible Conversations

[Peter Boghossian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Boghossian) and [James A. Lindsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Lindsay) wrote [How to Have Impossible Conversations](https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/peter-boghossian/how-to-have-impossible-conversations/9780738285320/) in 2019, the source of most of these techniques. They rest on older and better documented practice: [motivational interviewing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivational_interviewing), the [Socratic method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socratic_method), [street epistemology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_epistemology), and [Rapoport's rules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapoport%27s_rules). A brief and incomplete mnemonic:

- **Model it.** Be and do what you want them to do. Admit ignorance.
- **Watch words.** Be careful, and understand their definitions.
- **Ask questions.** Calibrated, open-ended how and what questions that do not lead to a simple yes or no.
- **Acknowledge extremists on your own side** to build a bridge across the moral divide. Concessions help, such as "some on my side are fanatics who should be arrested" or Democrats condemning [César Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesar_Chavez_sexual_abuse_allegations). Do not expect reciprocation; build trust. Treat their side charitably.
- **Do not blame.** Focus on contribution.
- **Focus on epistemology.** How do they know what they claim to know?
- **Learn what makes someone closed-minded.**

### Talking With a Conspiracist

[Michael Shermer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Shermer) gives a longer list in his 2022 book Conspiracy. It adds:

- **Channel Socrates.** Use [Socratic questions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socratic_questioning):
  - Clarity: "How do you know that's true?"
  - Sources: "What's your source for that?"
  - Evidence: "Is that all the evidence, or a selection?"
  - Other views: "What is another way to look at it?"
- **Ask for a number.** How certain are they, as a percentage?
- **Avoid the dishonest moves yourself.** They are questioning motives or authority, claiming a group's authority, changing the subject, and [sealioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sealioning). Sealioning buries a person in requests for evidence. Say "that idea", not "your idea".
- **Separate facts from worldviews.** A changed fact need not mean a changed [identity](../mind/identity-lightly.md).
- **Let people be wrong.** Friendship rests on respect, not agreement. [Jefferson](https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Jefferson/01-31-02-0445) wrote this in 1800. "I never considered a difference of opinion in politics, in religion, in philosophy, as cause for withdrawing from a friend."

==== Elite Rapture (Society) https://que.one/society/elite-rapture.html
Kind: take

## Elite Rapture

[Apocalypticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocalypticism) frames the present as the end times, with the world split into the righteous and the demonic. Some of its loudest voices today are wealthy tech figures, and I find that worth watching. [Peter Thiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel) has lectured on the [Antichrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antichrist) and cast [Greta Thunberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Thunberg) in that role, as [Gil Duran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Duran) reports in [The Nerd Reich](https://www.thenerdreich.com/peter-thiels-antichrist-circus-smacked-down-in-rome/). His [interview](https://youtu.be/KegSMO9XcIY) with [Robert C. Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_C._Fuller) places this in a long American tradition of end-times thinking. The same us-or-them framing runs through parts of the evangelical right.

My quarrel is with the framing, not the theology. Once the stakes are the end of the world, extreme measures feel not just justified but necessary. Compromise gets recast as part of the deception. Opponents stop being wrong and become less than human, and history is clear about where that leads. Every crusade needs a devil more than it needs a god. Whether planned or not, the story works as a tool of control that makes an agenda feel like a mandate.

The way out runs through the scripture these movements claim. Daniel and [Revelation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Revelation) are two books out of sixty-six. The rest is mostly a call to build a more just world and to love thy neighbor. The point was building, not tearing down. Powerful people have every reason to convince you the ending is already here.

==== Enlightenment Ideals (Society) https://que.one/society/enlightenment-ideals.html
Kind: note

## Enlightenment Ideals

[Steven Pinker](../mind/pinker.md) states the [Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment) ideal in one line: "we should use reason to improve human flourishing." He said it in a 2023 debate ([part one](https://youtu.be/SA-tCQJEzqk), [part two](https://youtu.be/gNVm-oXFK9k)) with the political scientist [John Mearsheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mearsheimer).

I hold the ideal as he states it, and I would like to think its core is the foundation of this site.

He spells out both halves of the line. Reason means [open deliberation](../mind/trust-in-truth.md), science, and history. Its fruits are institutions: liberal democracy, regulated markets, and international bodies. Flourishing is what each of us wants and cannot deny to others: life, health, sustenance, prosperity, peace, freedom, safety, knowledge, leisure, happiness.

He also says what the ideal is not. It is not reverence for some great men of the eighteenth century. "They were just guys." The ideas are what count. And it is not praise of the West, which "has always been ambivalent in its commitment" to it.

The rivals are old and still with us. Religion says we should obey God's commandments in holy scripture. Romantic nationalism says nations, embodied in strong leaders, should strive for historic greatness. Zero-sum struggle says subjugated groups must overcome their oppressors. Reactionary ideology says we should reject modernity and return to a golden age.

Mearsheimer's objection deserves its weight. Free reasoning, he says, does not bring people to agree on first principles or on the good life. It brings "significant disagreement", which is why politics matters. And people are social animals who belong to tribes, today called nations, with their identities bound up in them.

I think he is right about how people are. My own entries say as much: politics is [identity-first](us-identity-politics.md), and we [read facts through our groups](../mind/cultural-cognition.md). But that is a description. Pinker's line is an aim. The gap between what is and what ought to be, [Hume's guillotine](../mind/famous-lessons.md), is the space in which the ideal works. We are tribal, and we should reason anyway.

One caution of my own. Regulated markets are a fruit of reason, but defending them calls for care about historical timing. There are moments when the defense shades into [deference to money](money-exception.md).

==== The Immigration Choice (Society) https://que.one/society/immigration-choice.html
Kind: note

## The Immigration Choice

The case for mass deportation is that unenforced law invites more breaking of it, and that some towns carry costs they never agreed to. Drawing a line at the border is one thing. Removing millions of people who already live and work here is another, and I doubt it is feasible, affordable, or wise.

Start with the claim that undocumented immigrants overwhelm public benefits. Federal law bars them from nearly all [means-tested programs](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/blog/undocumented-immigrants-snap-medicaid-benefits/), including SNAP, Medicaid, TANF, and subsidized Affordable Care Act plans. Emergency care, school lunches, and a few other exceptions remain.

Meanwhile they pay in. The [Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy](https://itep.org/undocumented-immigrants-taxes-2024/), which favors progressive taxes, estimates they paid $96.7 billion in taxes in 2022. That included $25.7 billion into Social Security, which they cannot collect. Where a city's shelters or schools are strained, that reflects state and local capacity and funding, not a federal welfare transfer.

Now the cost of removal. The [American Immigration Council](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/report/mass-deportation/), which favors immigration, puts a one-time mass deportation at $315 billion or more. By the same report, undocumented workers make up about one in seven construction workers and one in eight agricultural workers. Remove them and labor gets scarcer and prices rise.

If the worry is that legal status invites more crossings, the answer is enforcement at the border and rules for the future. It is not expelling a workforce already woven into the economy.

What troubles me most is the cost in empathy. Harsh tactics draw support even from some people with immigrant roots of their own. Yet cruelty toward vulnerable families and children is hard to square with Christian ethics or with basic decency.

So the real choice is not open borders against lawlessness. It is whether we formalize and tax the people already here, or pay for an enforcement regime with uncertain returns. I would choose a structured, enforceable, conditional path to legal status. It strengthens compliance and widens the tax base.

==== Israel and Hamas (Society) https://que.one/society/israel-hamas.html
Kind: note

## Israel and Hamas

I lay out the two main framings of one debate here, with their sources, and take no position.

The debate over Israel's response to the 7 October 2023 attack in the [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war) turns on two charged words: genocide and disproportionality. Both have specific legal meanings. Both are also used in broader moral arguments. The human cost on both sides, above all to children, is why feeling overpowers analysis here. It is also why the line between legal and moral reasoning matters.

### The legal framing

[Sam Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Harris) argues in [5 Myths about Israel and the War in Gaza](https://www.samharris.org/blog/5-myths-about-israel-and-the-war-in-gaza) that the genocide charge is wrong in law and in fact. The [Genocide Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide_Convention) requires intent to destroy a group in whole or in part. He sees no such intent. He reads Gaza's long-term population growth as inconsistent with extermination.

On [proportionality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportionality_(international_humanitarian_law)) he notes that the standard is not a comparison of death counts. It asks whether expected civilian harm is excessive compared with the concrete military gain of a specific operation. Hamas placing fighters in civilian areas raises deaths without implying genocidal intent, he argues. And he holds that Israel is judged more harshly than other states in similar wars.

### The humanitarian framing

Critics answer that intent can be inferred from a pattern of conduct. The scale of civilian harm in dense urban war raises serious legal and ethical questions on its own. Narrow legalism, they say, separates technical compliance from what people are living through.

[Mehdi Hasan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan) argues in [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2025/aug/02/the-us-complicit-genocide-israel-gaza) that the conflict can be called genocide in law and in morals. He adds that United States political and material support makes it active participation. [Amnesty International](https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/mde15/8668/2024/en/) in December 2024, [Human Rights Watch](https://www.hrw.org/report/2024/12/19/extermination-and-acts-genocide/israel-deliberately-depriving-palestinians-gaza) the same month, and [B'Tselem](https://www.btselem.org/publications/202507_our_genocide) in July 2025 published reports. They concluded that Israel's conduct meets the definition of genocide or includes acts of genocide. The [Gaza genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_genocide) article on Wikipedia tracks the scholarly and legal record.

### The tension

Legal reasoning works from definitions, intent thresholds, and the limits of operations. Moral reasoning works from human cost and a sense of injustice. The legal framing's contribution is to force that distinction. The humanitarian framing's contribution is to insist that the distinction not become an excuse.

==== Libertarianism (Society) https://que.one/society/libertarianism.html
Kind: take

## Libertarianism

[Libertarianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarianism) puts individual liberty first and treats force by the state as the thing to minimize. It has real merits: doubt about concentrated power, respect for consent, and a check on paternalism. A popular modern strain extends that into body sovereignty. That is the position that personal choice outranks [public health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health) measures even during an epidemic, and it is the strain I take issue with.

That strain, whatever the intent behind it, is what I call [cold logic](../mind/cold-logic.md): a principle followed past the point where it stops serving people. The body-sovereignty position assumes everyone can make fully informed choices and absorb the consequences alone. That is not the world we live in. Most people do not have the knowledge, money, or medical access of a wealthy broadcaster. Promoting the ideal to an audience of millions during a pandemic shifts the risk onto them.

[Joe Rogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Rogan)'s public statements discouraging COVID-19 vaccination, documented on his Wikipedia page, are the clearest example of the position in action. The critique here is of the position, not the person.

A political philosophy has to account for [human limitations](../mind/reflexivity.md). Strong institutions exist because individuals cannot reason their way through every risk alone. A doctrine that ignores that cannot hold a society together.

==== Markets and Capitalism (Society) https://que.one/society/markets-capitalism.html
Kind: take

## Markets and Capitalism

Markets are systems for coordinating people, and I judge them that way. They reward innovation and pass information through [price signals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price_signal). They often allocate resources faster than [economic planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_planning). They coordinate millions without anyone holding all the information.

They also fail in known ways. Prices ignore [externalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Externality) such as pollution. Outcomes concentrate wealth and [bargaining power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bargaining_power) as output rises. Short-term incentives crowd out resilience and upkeep. And some goods distort when treated as products: attention, care, education, and political influence.

The question I find useful is never "markets or no markets". It is under what rules, incentives, and institutions markets produce outcomes worth wanting. Abstract models are incomplete. Real outcomes depend on human nature, institutional limits, cultural norms, and strategic behavior. That is why [game theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_theory) is part of the engine rather than a footnote.

So do not ask whether [capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism) is good or bad. Ask this. What incentives are being created? [Who captures the upside?](oligarchy.md) Who absorbs the downside? What rules would align private gain with public benefit?

Nor are markets the only engine of progress. [Charles Kenny](https://frompoverty.oxfam.org.uk/getting-better-why-global-development-is-succeeding-review-of-charles-kennys-new-book/) found that a country with no income growth for a century would still have seen [infant mortality](https://ourworldindata.org/child-mortality) fall by nearly two-thirds. Health, schooling, and rights spread through cheap technologies and ideas, even where incomes stalled. Growth is not all of progress.

Markets are tools, not moral oracles. They drive progress only under conditions. With weak rules and institutions they amplify extraction, inequality, and short-term thinking as easily.

==== Mild Leviathan (Society) https://que.one/society/mild-leviathan.html
Kind: take

## Mild Leviathan

[Hobbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leviathan_%28Hobbes_book%29) thought people would trade freedom for safety and hand a sovereign the sword. The [state of nature](../mind/core-challenges.md) he feared is real enough. But his cure was a monster, and every state since has had to be watched. I lean toward something milder, though I am not sure what.

[Elinor Ostrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom) showed that people who share a resource can write their own rules and keep them, without a sovereign or a sale. [Thaler and Sunstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian_paternalism) showed that a nudge can steer a choice while leaving the exit open. Both are mild Leviathans. The group gets the [slow thinking](../mind/two-systems.md) that no single member supplies, and consent stays with the member. That answers the [libertarian](libertarianism.md) objection, since nobody is forced.

What I add is speculative, and may be utopian. The [reflexivity](../mind/reflexivity.md) we lack could be supplied by an AI we contract with, one at a time, on the honor system. It would hold the pause, name the bias, and recall what we said last year. Self-governance assisted that way might work where slow institutions [cannot keep up](slow-by-design.md). The condition is an AI that is [aligned](../tech/before-agi.md) and has earned our trust, which is [Stuart Russell's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Compatible) whole problem.

My reading is that this is what separates the AI optimists from the [doomsayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risk_from_artificial_intelligence). Both see a Leviathan coming. The optimist thinks it can be kept mild, and volunteered. The doomsayer thinks no Leviathan stays mild. I am with the optimists for now, and every claim here has a sell-by date.

==== Internet Monetization Model (Society) https://que.one/society/monetization-model.html
Kind: note

## The Internet Monetization Model

The model I see behind most internet content businesses turns attention into revenue through one funnel: traffic, attention, trust, conversion, retention, expansion. It is a modern blend of the [purchase funnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchase_funnel), the [conversion funnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_funnel), [AIDA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDA_(marketing)), and [content marketing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_marketing). It applies to creators, software subscriptions, and online stores alike.

**Traffic** is bought as cheaply as possible from social platforms, search, and communities. It is high volume, low intent, and driven by algorithms. **Attention** keeps people consuming through feeds, short video, and endless scroll. Platforms tune this layer hardest because it comes before trust. **Trust** turns anonymous users into an audience through personality, direct contact, and steady value. Switching costs form here, and they are psychological rather than technical.

**Conversion** is the moment money changes hands: a subscription, a purchase, or a free-to-paid upgrade. It runs at one to five percent, a high-leverage point but not the main profit driver. **Retention** drives [lifetime value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customer_lifetime_value) through recurring billing and habit, and it decides whether the business is profitable. **Expansion** raises revenue per customer through upsells, cross-sells, and high-ticket offers.

Two versions dominate. Audience-first builds the audience and makes money later. It has high margins and the risk that the money never comes. Product-first builds the product and buys users. It is predictable and expensive.

Ad-funded platforms sell attention directly and skip conversion. Marketplaces depend on liquidity more than on funnels. Search-driven businesses compress the funnel because intent already exists.

The first sale is not where value is created. Profit comes from retention and expansion. The rest of the funnel exists to feed them.

### Recommendation systems

The attention layer is run by [recommender systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommender_system) tuned to keep you on the platform. Time on the platform is what gets sold to advertisers. The engineers are not villains. They are answering a business incentive, and video feeds, social networks, and 24-hour cable news all run the same model.

The political cost is that the tuning rewards whatever is vivid and stirs feeling. That is how [Pizzagate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pizzagate_conspiracy_theory) spread. How that shapes belief is the subject of [perception management](perception-management.md). What it does to political identity is in [identity politics](us-identity-politics.md).

==== The Money Exception (Society) https://que.one/society/money-exception.html
Kind: note

## The Money Exception

In 2011 [Sam Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Harris) found the one thing his readers would not forgive. He could call the world's religions "cesspools of confusion and bigotry", deny free will, even defend torture, he wrote, and keep his audience. Then he [suggested](https://www.samharris.org/blog/how-rich-is-too-rich) that billionaires pay more tax. "Nothing will rile and winnow your audience" like that, he [reported afterward](https://www.samharris.org/blog/how-to-lose-readers-without-even-trying). He called the reaction a "quasi-religious abhorrence of 'wealth redistribution'".

I see a quieter version among thinkers I admire. [Steven Pinker](../mind/pinker.md) argues in [Enlightenment Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlightenment_Now) that economic inequality "is not itself a dimension of human wellbeing".
